speechtext: Order. May I recall to the house that the national film board endeavoured to get a picture of the house in session some two or three weeks ago without using flashlights. maintopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT DIVERSION AND DUMPING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT DIVERSION AND DUMPING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Is the government considering action which might counteract the effect on Canadian oil production arising out of the pressures created by the new oil restrictions in the United States for the diversion and dumping into Canada of oil and its products which would otherwise have been exported to the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT DIVERSION AND DUMPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject is a matter of very great concern to the government and to the oil industry in Canada, as well as to all Canadians. We have the matter under review, and close study is being made of the mandatory controls recently set up by Washington. In due course we perhaps will have something to say with regard to what may be done. At this time, however,
I may say that the whole problem of the oil industry is certainly seriously affected by the controls which have been established. There has been some leeway permitted in the midwestern area of the United States, to which area some of our crude oil has been going. The government recognizes the serious situation that now prevails.

speechtext: So far as I know, no request as yet has been made in that connection. When any communication is received the matter will receive consideration. subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: May I ask a question supplementary to the question I asked the Prime Minister. I now ask the same question of the Minister of Justice.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have seen the report in this morning's Gazette that Mr. Jodoin is sending me a formal request. I have not seen it myself, but I have been informed that it has been delivered to my office in the justice building just recently, and that it does ask that we conduct some sort of formal inquiry into the activities of the R.C.M. police in Newfoundland.
I have to say in reply that I am told by my office that the letter contains no specific information to back up the allegation that the R.C.M. police have acted in an improper manner. I have had no such evidence from elsewhere, and in the absence of such evidence I would not feel inclined to recommend to my colleagues that such an inquiry be held. However, if evidence is received, or if factual information is received that would warrant it, we would immediately reconsider the position.

Furthermore, as soon as the situation down there permits the ordinary administrative routine to be resumed I would expect to be receiving full and detailed reports of every one of the incidents involved, and if those reports themselves disclose anything that would warrant such an inquiry I shall refer the matter to my colleagues for a decision.
But at the moment there is no evidence or information before me which would lead me to change the opinion I have expressed to the house that the R.C.M. police have conducted themselves with restraint under very difficult circumstances.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: A supplementary question. We are all interested in peace and harmony and a solution to this difficulty. I would like to ask the Minister of Justice whether he is in a position to go to Newfoundland personally and see what can be done to solve the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am as concerned as anyone in the house, but no more concerned certainly than any of my colleagues, and probably no more concerned than other hon. members. While I have every desire to do everything possible to contribute to a settlement of this question, the question of anyone visiting Newfoundland would obviously have to be a governmental decision. This matter has not yet been taken up because there seems to be no occasion for it; there has been no suggestion that such a visit would produce any good results.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: May I ask another supplementary question. Is the Minister of Labour interesting himself in the situation, and is it possible for his good offices to be used in Newfoundland?

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member well knows, as every member in the house knows, that this matter is strictly under provincial jurisdiction and the federal Department of Labour has no jurisdiction at all in this dispute.

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext: I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Justice. When the minister is making the survey of R.C.M.P. activities in Newfoundland will he find out whether I.W.A. property was given the same protection by the R.C.M.P., on the occasion when windows were broken, as was given to the property of the company on other occasions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
subsubtopic: REQUEST OF LABOUR CONGRESS FOR INVESTIGATION INTO LABOUR DISPUTE FATALITY
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the reports I will be receiving will cover the situation.
I should perhaps advise the hon. member that I have an interim report this morning

that yesterday, in the course of transporting the body of the constable who was killed back to St. John's for burial, at one of the small towns through which the train passed there was a demonstration which took the form later of an attack on the I.W.A. hall in that community. Before the situation could be brought under control there was, I understand, some damage done to the hall; but as soon as possible the police moved in and were able to restore the situation and bring about a cessation of the attacks without the necessity of using force. The police moved just as quickly as possible to protect that property, in the same way that they will move to protect any property that may come under danger.

speechtext:

carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I was hoping that the Minister of Justice would be present in the committee, because my observations relate to his conduct rather than to that of the hon. lady. I should like to make one or two observations about what the hon.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration lady very properly called a fiasco as revealed by the questions asked last evening by the Leader of the Opposition.
The observation I want to make is this. It appeared from what the Leader of the Opposition brought out last night and from what the hon. lady herself said in the answer she gave in parliament that the government were perfectly prepared to buy the picture in question so long as they thought there was an existing appropriation, and it probably would not come to the notice of parliament; but when they found that they would have to come here in a straightforward manner and ask parliament to vote the money-
Oh, oh.
-they backed down on their commitment. The record shows that very clearly indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Utter rubbish.
The Minister of Finance, who was probably at that time on one of his numerous travels instead of attending to his business here in Canada, failed

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Wrong again.
-according to the record-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Too bad you
couldn't be right once in a while.

According to the record, or at least according to the evidence that has been supplied so far and is uncontradicted, the government were quite prepared to buy this picture if there had been an appropriation, but when they found that they would have to come in here and in a straightforward, honest fashion ask parliament to vote money, they repudiated the good name of Canada. This is what happened, and there is no getting away from it.
Perhaps the most shocking feature of all, sir, is that the Minister of Finance, who presumably was represented at the cabinet meeting if he was not there himself, ought to have known what the appropriations were. In other days the affairs of this country were managed differently.
They sure were.

The Minister of Finance did know, in those days what was going on in government and commitments were not made that had to be repudiated because of misunderstandings about the real situation. It does seem to me, sir, that this is a shocking and a shabby business. It is quite obvious that what the government hoped to be able to do was buy this picture and then, if there was any criticism, get up and say that the Liberals had provided the money. However,

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration after finding they had to come in here and take the responsibility for their own act, they did not have the courage to do so. What they very obviously decided to do-

May I ask
a question-
This is a beautiful example of the kind of government we have been getting during the last two years.

May I ask a
question? Would the hon. gentleman have been prepared to spend this amount of money himself, if he had been in the position to make the decision?
Well, that would have depended upon-
Oh, oh.

-that would have depended entirely upon the state of the exchequer. As the hon. gentleman knows, in the days when we were in office we had a very considerable surplus because the affairs of this country were being well managed. We could well afford to purchase imperishable articles of this sort that would last as long as the country lasts. We are not ashamed of having done so. However, if the country had got into the terrible condition financially that it has under the hon. gentlemen opposite, I doubt if it would have been a prudent thing to do.
I did not have that decision to make. The decision had to be made by the Minister of Justice, as acting minister, by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. I feel sorry for the Minister of Justice because having made a commitment on behalf of the government of Canada, and knowing the Minister of Justice as I do, I am sure he wanted to keep it. I am sure he was overruled by his colleagues. I am sympathetic toward the Minister of Justice, and I am sorry for him. I am sorry to see this habit of repudiation beginning to develop.
I am sorry to see the Minister of Justice being put in the false position in which he has been put over this matter. It does seem to me, sir, that either the government should have decided in the first place they were not going to spend this money, if indeed they were so concerned about the treasury as they later pretended to be, and made a decision on the basis of the merits of the case. However, having made a decision and then having found they were wrong about the technicalities, they should have been honest enough and straightforward enough to go through with what they had started.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not lost his ability to work up a fine state of frenzy over nothing.
Just a repudiation of contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is quite obvious that the hon. gentleman wishes to continue in opposition that great fault from which the Liberal government suffered when in office; that was to commit the country to a course for which they had no authority, and to act as a government in a manner for which they had not been given any authority by the house. Now the hon. gentleman has asked us to do the same thing, which we refuse to do, and for the doing of which the previous government was, in a large measure, repudiated by the country. The fact of the matter is that no commitment was made because there was no authority to make any commitment.
That is not what the hon. lady says.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. lady said so, as will be found on the record at page 1905 of Hansard for March 12, 1959. She said:
It is clear that no authority existed to make a firm offer or enter into a contract for this purchase by the national gallery or the government of Canada or anyone on its or their behalf.
The hon. member knows, and I assume has conveniently forgotten for the purpose of this discussion, that in the absence of an appropriation by parliament there can be no contract, and that in the absence of an appropriation by parliament no one has any authority to make a contract. Hence what the hon. gentleman is asking us to do or is suggesting that we should have done is to make a contract for which we had no authority. When we found that was the position we informed all those concerned immediately, explained the position and said that we were not prepared, in the absence of parliamentary authority, to do that which we had no authority to do; nor were we prepared, as the former government so often did, to seek to commit parliament as to what parliament would do, before parliament had any opportunity to express its opinion.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that completely disposes of the matter except to say this. If any further answer were required the hon. gentleman has given it himself. When, after all the sound and fury which he emitted, he was asked a simple question, namely whether if he had the authority, he would have come to parliament for the appropriation, he took refuge in those typical Liberal words, "That would depend upon the circumstances". What a fine ending for an

initially valiant stand. Having started out so valiantly to do battle, when he sees the enemy he turns tail and flees.

If any hon. member has ever seen me turn tail and flee in this house, Mr. Chairman, I should like him to cite the occasion. What I said about the hon. gentleman, which he cleverly-because he is clever -perverted in his reply, was that the government should not have entered into these negotiations at all if it did not intend to go through with them. I said, and I repeat, that it was extremely incompetent of the minister and of the government not to know the facts, not to know whether there was an appropriation before they entered upon these negotiations. That was the whole point. It is just another of the examples we have had over and over again in the last two years of the fumbling and bumbling incompetence of the present administration.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps in a quiet mood I could ask a few questions which might help to get to the truth of this matter. At page 1364 of Hansard, in her answer to the question, the minister stated:
-the board of trustees of the national gallery had asked for "authorization to negotiate for the purchase of the Breughel owned by Baron von Polnitz".
This is my first question, and I have many more. Will the minister tell me from what that quotation is taken? Perhaps she would put the full communication on the record. Will she also give us the date when that authorization was requested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer that question, Mr. Chairman, because I was acting minister at the time. The quotation reproduced at page 1364 of Hansard comes from a resolution of the trustees of the national gallery. In this resolution it was stated- I am not sure that I am quoting the language exactly but I know that the fact is correct; it was in either that resolution or the immediately preceding one to which it was related -that funds were appropriated for the purpose. Then the resolution went on to ask the government to give authority to negotiate in the terms which are quoted at page 1364 of Hansard.
With regard to the previous statements of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, it would take a long time to correct all his inaccuracies, but there is one that I think should be corrected. The government at no time entered into negotiations. The government authorized negotiations to be commenced on the basis of the information it had received from responsible persons appointed by the previous government to manage the affairs of this gallery.
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Does the Minister of Justice deny that negotiations in regard to the purchase of this picture had been going on for weeks before the communication from the gallery to which he has referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not in a position to confirm or deny that. I find that at page 1903 of yesterday's Hansard the hon. gentleman himself is reported as having said:
If I am inaccurate in giving my account of these negotiations no doubt the minister, who has the records at her disposal, will correct me. As I understand the situation, the first contact between a representative of the gallery and the agent for the owner of the picture, a landscape by Breughel, was made on January 4, 1957.
If that date is correct it would, of course, be during the administration of the hon. gentleman and his friends who were then in office.

That information is quite correct. The first approach was made at that time. Does the minister not agree that subsequent to that time, as I mentioned last night, at the end of the year, or in January 1958 these negotiations regarding the purchase of this picture were proceeding and that negotiations had gone so far that prices were being discussed, as to what would be a fair value for the picture? Is not that negotiation, and is not that long before the statement from the gallery to which the minister has referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The matter first came to my knowledge in about February of 1958, as I recall it, when the director of the gallery first gave me a resolution of the trustees. That was a resolution of the trustees of January 29, 1958. The trustees were then meeting, and immediately after that meeting *-I think it was early in February; within the first few days of February-the director brought this resolution to my attention and first asked for authority to negotiate. That authority was not given at that time. It was late January, or early February, when I was first advised by the director that discussions-I do not think they should properly be called negotiations-had been entered into between representatives of the gallery and representatives of the owner of the painting with regard to possible purchase.

I will not quibble over the
difference between the words "discussion" and "negotiation". The minister now admits that in February he knew discussions were going on with regard to the possible purchase of this painting. I ask the minister now whether this matter was not brought by him before the cabinet, and whether there was not a discussion of this matter by the cabinet. I ask him when that discussion took place, and whether there was not an agreement

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration reached by the cabinet that an offer of $350,000 should be made for this picture.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, that is incorrect. The
matter was brought before the cabinet by me on the basis of a resolution of the board of trustees requesting "that cabinet document 244/53 of October 7, 1953, be amended so that the sum of $2 million appropriated for the purchase of paintings from the collection of the Prince of Liechtenstein, of which $441,000 remains, could be applied to the purchase of works of comparable quality and importance". That was the resolution of January 29 which the director requested me to take to the cabinet. The request was taken to the cabinet, and on that occasion the cabinet turned it down.

So was not the directorand he must have been acting in his capacity as director; the gallery is a department of government in this regard-authorized on May 2 to make an offer to the agent of the owner for the purchase of this picture?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On the second occasion when
the submission was brought forward the cabinet approved it. The submission was based on the resolution of the trustees asking for authority to negotiate, and the director was advised that the cabinet had approved.

I am asking the minister
whether the director was authorized to make an offer to the owner for the purchase of this picture at an amount of $350,000 or some other amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The authority that had been
asked for was authority to find out whether two paintings could be bought. It was asked that authority be given to negotiate to find out if one painting could be bought for a certain price and, if it could, it could be that authority would be given to negotiate for the other painting to see if it could be bought for a certain price. The resolution asked for authority to negotiate, and it was a submission based on this resolution which was approved by the cabinet.

The minister now says there was no authority given to any representative of the gallery to make an offer at that time, May 2, for the purchase of this picture. I follow this up by asking him whether such an offer was made to the agent of the owner of this picture, a firm offer, without strings, at a particular price?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as the Breughel is concerned, I was advised by the director of the gallery that he inquired of the agent of the owner whether the owner would be willing to sell for that price. I was advised by the director in a memorandum from him that this was

the question he asked, whether the owner would sell the Breughel for $350,000. It appears that this inquiry, this conversation, was taken by the agent as a firm offer. What justification the agent had for doing so I fail to understand. The position is, as I have said, that there was no authority to make an offer. The only authority given was to negotiate. There could have been no authority to make an offer or enter into a contract, because there had been no appropriation.
The minister now states very clearly that there was no authority given to make an offer for the purchase of this picture, and that so far as he knows no offer was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No offer, on the basis of this memorandum of the conversation which I have received; no offer which I as a lawyer would regard as a firm offer.
Well I, perhaps, would make a distinction between an offer which would be regarded as a firm offer by a lawyer and an offer which might be regarded as a firm offer by the owner of the picture.
Oh, oh.
I ask the minister this. Was the owner of this picture, who was acting in good faith in this matter-
How do you know?
I know a little more about this than the hon. gentleman does, so perhaps he will not bother to interrupt. Was the owner of this picture not asked to confirm his acceptance of the offer in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will have to check the documents and memoranda again. My information is that it was the owner who asked whether what he describes as the offer could be confirmed in writing, and the owner was notified on May 8 that the basis for any further negotiations no longer existed. I think it was on May 8; certainly it was not later than May 12.

I think it is a fact that the minister saw the agent for the owner of this picture on May 8. Did the minister at that time tell the agent that he had previously obtained agreement to make the offer on the understanding that the money was available, and that later he found he was wrong in this understanding and that he did not wish to ask parliament for the appropriation which would now be required.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is asking me to recall a conversation which I am frankly unable to do in detail at the moment. I recall the agent visiting me in my office, at which time I explained the position to him in detail and explained that there had been no legal

basis on which any offer could be made. I also said that I could not hold out for him any hope that the government would decide to go before parliament and ask for an appropriation, and that in the absence of an appropriation there was no authority for anyone to commit the government. I told him 1 would consider the situation further, but that I could not hold out any hope of an outcome that would be acceptable to the agent.
May I ask the minister when and how the government finally decided that the money was not available unless a further appropriation was made by parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My recollection is that the absence of an appropriation was first confirmed on May 7, some three days after the submission had been approved by the cabinet, when I was asked to make a submission to treasury board asking that an item be inserted in the supplementary estimates for an appropriation.

From what we have learned, Mr. Chairman, the minister I know will agree with my statement that a representative of the government, the director of the gallery, was authorized to negotiate for the purchase of this picture, which was an important negotiation both financially and otherwise, on the assumption that $350,000 was available when it was not in fact available.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The director was authorized to negotiate on that basis; that is a correct statement of the facts. I have referred to two resolutions of the trustees stating that the funds were available. I should also mention that on several occasions when the matter was under discussion I questioned the director of the gallery as to whether in fact the funds were available, and I was assured that they were.

Then later the owner, assuming this was a serious negotiation, was told there was no such financial basis for negotiation. May I ask when the owner was finally and officially informed that the government was not going to proceed with the purchase of this picture?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the owner was informed?
I should like to know when the owner was finally and officially informed that the government did not intend to proceed with the purchase of the picture.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as being a government decision I would have to ask my colleague who is presently the minister concerned to answer that. My recollection is clear that there was a telephone call on the 8th and a letter from the director to the agent on the 12th. I ceased to be acting minister on the 14th. I believe I actually handed over to my
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration colleague, the present minister, on May 21. I have recounted the interview I had with the agent, at which time I told him I could see no way in which the matter could be proceeded with; but whether there were further official letters from the minister or on behalf of the government stating this as a government decision, I would have to leave the present minister to answer.
As I have said, there was a letter from the director to the agent on May 12. There was a visit from the agent to myself within a very few days of that time; it may have been within a week or ten days. I recall also that later I had a discussion with a solicitor who I understood was retained by the owner or the agent, I am not sure which. I understand he also had some conversation with my colleague, but I am not sure of that. He came to me because I had been acting minister at the time.
Certainly on the basis of those discussions I told him that the government's decision was that there was no way of proceeding with it, that we did not intend to proceed, and the solicitor agreed that there was no contract. We have not heard further from the solicitor since that time.

One final question, Mr. Chairman. Has the owner made an effort to see the Prime Minister or any minister, and has there been any such interview between the owner and any representative of the government on this matter?

Possibly I could answer that, Mr. Chairman. I understand the owner was in town. I was given to understand there would be some attempt made to have an appointment with the Prime Minister or with this minister. Certainly no approaches were made to this minister, and I understand the situation is precisely the same with regard to the Prime Minister, but of course I cannot answer for him.

Mr. Chairman, just a few brief remarks on this item. Mr. Chairman, I have only one question to ask the hon. lady, and I am not going to inflict any speech on the committee. I think it would be of great interest to the public if the hon. lady could tell us the progress that is being made in dealing with the public records of the various departments, reducing their volume and getting them into the public records office; because in my opinion this is one of the most important functions the archives are carrying on at the present time. It could save the Minister of Public Works millions and millions of dollars in real estate if it is done quickly and efficiently. If the hon. lady could make a statement I would be greatly pleased.

Mr. Chairman, the reason I did not rise immediately is that, as the hon. member knows, the work of the public archives is very diverse and to attempt to summarize it in brief form is almost impossible in
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration a short space of time. I am anxious to answer any specific questions which the members may have, but I do have a statement with regard to the records centre which I shall be very glad to read.
The records centre, which is one of the group of government buildings at Tunney's pasture in Ottawa West, was handed over to the archives on January 3, 1956. It was formally opened on April 10, after the installation of shelving and other essential equipment. The building is approximately 200 feet square and there are five storeys. Floor area totals more than four acres. Initially, 20 miles of steel shelving were installed; another 20 miles were added in 1957.

speechtext: Order. I wonder whether hon. members would keep their voices down. It is hard to hear the minister when she is speaking.
Would the hon. lady read a little more slowly for the benefit of the duller members of the committee like me?

I shall certainly comply with the suggestion. I know, Mr. Chairman, that is a fault of mine; I am inclined to speak too quickly.
When all the filing rooms are fully equipped the building will have 62 miles of shelving. In addition to file rooms, the centre has receiving and sorting rooms, a fumigating chamber, offices, reference rooms and a research room. It is thus a fully equipped branch of the public archives, with all necessary reference and research facilities.
The primary purpose of the centre is to take over from departments and agencies all records that are not required for day to day use. Such records can be divided, in a rough and ready way, into "dead" files and "dormant" files. As the name implies, the former are referred to seldom, if ever. In the records centre they are examined and their future determined, in consultation with the department in which they originated. The department advises with regard to their practical value, or lack of it; the archives determine whether or not they contain material of long term importance or historic interest. Files that are retained for departmental use are filed in the records centre; those of historical importance will ultimately be transferred to the public archives building.
Useless material is disposed of through the public records committee, established by order in council in 1945. Particulars of the files for disposal are submitted to the committee; if the committee concurs in the recommendation that they should be destroyed it in turn recommends their destruction to treasury board. Although experience indicates that
1922	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration large quantities of old records can be destroyed and much valuable space and equipment thereby freed for further use, due care is taken to see that files of interest or importance are not disposed of. As the procedure outlined indicates, every proposal to destroy "dead" records must pass scrutiny from the departmental, historical, financial and legal points of view.
Files are considered to be in the "dormant" category if, on the average, references to them are not more frequent than one reference per file drawer per month. Much of the "dormant" material that has been transferred to the records centre must be referred to occasionally by the department from which it came, and the reference staff of the centre will either check a file or return the file itself to the department on loan, whichever the department prefers. In many instances additional files are transferred to the centre from time to time which must be integrated with the files already there; these "interfiles" must be handled with care and accuracy, and they are an important aspect of the service offered to departments by the records centre.
Inventories and detailed accession lists of all records transferred to the centre are compiled for the information of both the departments and the archives. These lists are so arranged that if they are merely given the file number under which a document was filed in a departmental registry, the staff of the centre can find quickly and accurately any one amongst the hundreds of thousands of individual documents that have been placed in their keeping. Quick access to records in the centre can thus be guaranteed, and this is naturally an important consideration to departments that send their files to it.
The following statistics summarize the activities of the records centre in the first three years of its operation: Cubic feet of records accessioned, in 1956, 53,471; in 1957, 29,007; in 1958, 31,242; square feet of floor space cleared in other buildings-and this is with reference to my hon. friend's remarks -46,291 in 1956; in 1957, 21,609; in 1958, 19,742. Requests for loans of files received from departments were 3,777 in 1956, 15,404 in 1957 and 35,958 in 1958. In other words, in three years the number of such requests increased over eleven times. Interfiles numbered 1,421 in 1956, 7,838 in 1957 and 63,715 in 1958, which is an indication of the increasing use being made of the records centre by the various departments of government. Cubic feet of records destroyed amounted to 240 in 1956, 7,425 in 1957 and 4,648 in 1958.
Up to December 31, 1958, the centre had thus received 113,720 cubic feet of records and had cleared a total of 87,642 square feet


of floor space, or more than two acres, in offices, filing rooms, vaults, basements, attics and storage rooms in other buildings. These records came from 28 departments and agencies of the government. Much of the material transferred was placed in special cardboard cartons that are cheap, reasonably dustproof, and use the space on the centre's shelves to maximum advantage. As a result, large quantities of filing equipment were released, much of which could be used again by the departments. In the three year period, 13,881 transfer cases and 5,377 filing cabinet.' were released in this way.
Except in a few instances it seems probable that most departments and agencies have now sent to the centre the bulk of the dead and dormant records that were causing acute crowding and space problems. The next step will be to persuade them to make the regular transfer of their older files to the records centre an integral part of their whole registry and records systems. Onl; in this way can the full benefit of the facilities and economies offered by the centre be secured. Careful planning will be necessary to bring this about; and in December, 1958, the public records committee appointed a small investigating committee with a view to securing for the committee and the archives the data necessary to plan for the future from a long term point of view.
In 1957, at the request of treasury board, the records centre undertook the task of assembling, sorting, culling and filing all personnel records relating to men and women who have been in the civil service but who ceased to be employed, for one reason or another, at least three years ago. This is a complicated undertaking, and among other things involves bringing together files held by the civil service commission, the superannuation branch of the Department of Finance, and all employing departments and agencies. Good progress is being made and files are now being processed at the rate of about 12,000 per month.

Mr. Chairman, when the debate on the agricultural estimates was interrupted at five o'clock last Friday for the consideration of private and public bills I had just finished my presentation regarding the freight rate on rapeseed. Today I should like to speak about the tariff on rape seed. At the present time our tariff structure allows soybean oil, the largest competitor of rapeseed oil, to enter Canada from the United States under a 20 per cent tariff. However, soybeans themselves can be brought in duty free. Beans are transported into Canada, processed here and the oil sold on the Canadian market. The Canadian processor may also ship the oil back into the United States duty free or export the oil and meal under the British preferential tariff provided they have 25 per cent Canadian content.
Cottonseed oil, peanut oil and corn oil all enter Canada duty free. On the other hand, although there is no tariff with respect to Canadian rapeseed being sold in the United States, the rapeseed is subject to a 1 cent per pound import tax. Canadian rapeseed meal going into the United States is subject to a tariff of $6 per ton. So, Mr. Chairman, I know hon. members will agree with me in my presentation of the story of rapeseed.
I should like to turn now to another subject. At this time we hear so much in my province and in the west as a whole about

the high cost of production and the cost-price squeeze. Nobody can deny the fact that the farmers of the west are labouring under these conditions and that the federal government has done many things since 1957 to eliminate them. Many more such steps will be forthcoming, some in the near future and others at a later date. But we cannot remedy all the existing evils and shortcomings of the past in one year.
This accounts for the delegation from the west. The march to Ottawa this week was very orderly. The 1,100 delegates from the west who came here were anxious to bring their case personally to the attention of the government. They behaved like gentlemen and were given a most friendly reception and hearing by the cabinet and members generally.
In the brief submitted to the government they stressed deficiency payments and the two price system for wheat. Of course the government has had no opportunity so far of reviewing the brief or coming to any decision. Serious consideration will have to be given to the contents of the brief. Personally I cannot disapprove of the stand our western farmers have taken at this time, as they are only requesting a fair share of our national income, which other sectors of our economy are securing.
However, I hasten to say that the situation in which our western farmers find themselves today is not one that came into being today, this year or last year. It had its start many years ago and has deteriorated over the last five or six years, to the point where it has become ruinous to many of our farmers. Nothing was done in the past by our predecessors to stem the tide of the cost-price squeeze or even to slow it down. Had steps been taken four or five years ago; or had full support been given to farm organizations which had prepared proposals for presentation to federal authorities, and had those proposals been given unanimous support by all farm organizations and farmers, as is being done today, some of our farm problems would have been solved years ago.
If the situation is considered to be a legitimate case now, why was it not a legitimate case then when the situation was similar to or worse than the one we are experiencing today? It was apparent to everyone in the west at that time that the situation could not continue any longer, but no attempt was made at that time to alleviate the situation or to make representations to the government in power at that time. I can only say now, let this be a lesson to us, and an example. If we, as representatives in this

Supply-Agriculture
house of western agriculture, must speak and act for western agriculture, let us do so with a unanimous voice and without prejudice or discrimination whatever. We will have to stand up for the sacred rights of our farmers. Let us be worthy of those men who stood up in the past and asked only for equal rights and consideration, for a fair share of the national income.
We who represent the farmers in this parliament relentlessly work conscientiously toward this goal. Our government has done a tremendous job since 1957. The records and figures are there for everybody to see. New legislation has been enacted, old statutes have been revised and amended, with only one aim in mind; that is to do all that is humanly possible to alleviate the plight of the western grain farmer and bring the cost of production in line with his income.
In conclusion I should like to say we should not only be concerned with the present situation, but we should also be concerned about the future of Canada and the long range programs for agriculture, so that all problems coming before this house will receive sympathetic and fair consideration. We ask that a just hearing be given to all representations and briefs, so that all decisions will be made without prejudice or discrimination against any one segment of our nation. This is our task, and I am sure our government will complete it to the full extent of their capabilities.

Representing as I do a largely agricultural riding in the province of Quebec, I shall, naturally, limit my remarks to the problems facing the eastern farmers. Not that the problems of the westerners are unimportant. On the contrary, western agriculture, by its very character, affects the economy of the whole country. However, I shall leave it to hon. members from the west to deal with their own problems.
In the province of Quebec, there are no large farms as in the west, but agriculture remains nevertheless, a very basic industry.
In 1951, Quebec had a population about three times as large as in 1901, and yet from a percentage point of view fewer people were farming than in 1901.

According to a news letter published by the Banque Canadienne Nationale in April 1958, there were 60 rural people against 40 city dwellers at that time, whereas in 1951, the ratio was 33 to 67. Between 1941 and 1956, our rural population has decreased by some

Mr. Chairman, last Friday, an hon. member stated that the speech of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) was a liability for the agricultural class. Besides, that is what is stated in the final report of the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects, on page 175:
Too easy credit can aggravate farm problems by inducing an expansion in output that would lead to lower prices.
Scarcity of credit, on the other hand, can prevent a desirable rise in agricultural productivity by perpetuating antiquated types of farm organization. As the mechanization of Canadian farms continues, some farmers in all parts of the country will need more medium-term capital to enable them to buy machinery and equipment, and more long-term capital to enable them to enlarge their holdings, while the rise in demand for meat will mean that more capital will also be needed for the purchase of livestock. As the result of these cumulative developments, the capital value of farm businesses will be rising on the average; and there will be difficulty in transferring them from one owner to another-in many cases it will be from father to son-unless somewhat more generous credit arrangements are available. So long as farm incomes are relatively low and irregular, it is important that fixed annual payments on mortgages and other forms of indebtedness be no larger than is necessary. Appropriate rates of interest will vary from time to time, but annual payments can be reduced by extending the number of years over which the principal will be repaid. Since the long-range prospects for farm income and for the ability of farmers to service loans would seem to be favourable, we think that farm credit agencies might appropriately extend the period of repayment up to 40 years for long-term loans and up to five or six years for medium-term loans. Extension of credit on somewhat easier terms is one way by which the adjustment of Canadian farming to changing economic conditions can be facilitated.
The price support legislation passed by the former government, and the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act passed by the present government, have been greatly beneficial to farmers. But are those two acts adequate to give farmers all the guarantees they are entitled to? Probably not.
It is necessary that a commission be set up to study production costs of various agricultural products, and perhaps to find a way of producing and marketing such products somewhat more economically.
Statistics show that it has been possible to increase production while cutting down labour, and I wonder whether a commission set up to enquire into production costs might not have the same happy results, namely to supply farmers with scientific and technical production data, because if production costs could be lowered, farmers would be able to raise their profits and could offer for sale on the international market a number of products that the national market cannot fully absorb.
Farmers have always shown their willingness to co-operate, and the most striking

As soon as, in any area, farmers and settlers agree on a joint plan, a remarkable thing happens: companies stop buying pulpwood. understanding with the companies having concessions and oblige them to purchase part of their requirements from farmers.

In the period 1948-1955, which is the period covered by the report, pulpwood purchases from all sources for use by the pulp and paper industry in Eastern Canada comprised between 26.7 and 34.6 per cent of such usage in the province of Quebec and between 30.9 and 39.9 per cent of such usage in the province of Ontario. The commission noted that: "for the pulp and paper industry as a whole, farmers' pulpwood constitutes probably less than 25 per cent of the total pulpwood used."

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to advise the house that successful talks have been held between Canadian and United States officials who met in Ottawa on March 12 and 13 to discuss modification of the bilateral air agreement of June 4, 1949, as amended.
The discussions concentrated for the most part on improving present trans-border routes so as to provide a better service to the travelling public of both countries. The delegations expressed the hope that the discussions would be resumed at an early date to review the air traffic requirements of the two countries on a broader basis.
The two delegations agreed to recommend to their respective governments the following improved services. Canadian carriers may operate between (1) Prince Rupert and Ketchikan; (2) Calgary and Spokane; (3) Winnipeg and/or Kenora, International Falls and Fort William-Port Arthur; (4) Toronto and Buffalo; (5) Halifax and New York by an extension of the Halifax-Boston route.
United States carriers may operate between (1) Ketchikan and Prince Rupert; (2) Spokane and Calgary; (3) Great Falls and Calgary in replacement for Lethbridge on the existing Great Falls-Edmonton route; (4) Minot and Regina; (5) Duluth-Superior, Fort William-Port Arthur and Hancock-Houghton; (6) Buffalo and Toronto.
It was also agreed that a United States carrier might serve Portland, Maine, as an intermediate stop on the existing route between Boston and Montreal and that

Winnipeg might be served on present U.S. turnaround flights between Minneapolis-St. Paul and Edmonton. This agreement will be put into effect, when approved by each government, by an exchange of diplomatic notes.

Mr. Chairman, in years past we have heard it said that many of the members from eastern and central Canada are not familiar with agriculture and these members have had to listen, without knowing too much about agriculture, to other members discuss the subject. However, I think that cannot be said now of the present membership of the House of Commons because during this week we have had the opportunity to hear a number of western farmers present a specific problem.
It may be quite true that the industrial sections of Ontario are not too concerned with the matter but I do not think it can be said any longer that they do not understand some of the problems facing farmers across Canada and particularly the grain producers of western Canada. Over the years politicians on both sides of the house have supported the need of establishing a closer relationship between the cost of the goods the farmer must buy in order to produce and the amount of money he gets for his product. When the Prime Minister and other ministers of the government sat in the opposition they pointed out the need to establish a fair relationship between the cost of production and the selling price of the product. This has not been put into effect and is not being put into effect at the present time. It is true that some slight consideration has been given to the matter under the Agricultural Stabilization Act but in general no consideration has been given to establishing parity prices for farm products.
I am sure that the farmers of western Canada are well aware-the delegates I spoke to were-of the need to establish a fair and just situation so that as their production costs rise they will be able to justify their position when they ask more from consumers in the rest of Canada for what they produce. I should like to congratulate the people responsible for the delegation. Their manner was certainly controlled, quiet and dignified. They presented their arguments to the government and to members generally in an orderly and reserved fashion. I think they were a credit to the people they represent and made the contribution they came here to make.
It was stated by a number of members that this delegation was not necessary. It would have been fine to send only two or three people down to represent them. I am quite sure if that had been the method chosen

Supply-Agriculture
the delegates would have made a fair representation. I am quite sure that the
300,000	people who supported this delegation, who gave money to pay the expenses involved in the delegation, are going to find much more satisfaction in being able to talk to their delegate and hear firsthand of the reception he received in Ottawa. I think these people are going to be anxious to find out if there was any difference in the attitude of the government between the time the delegation arrived in Ottawa and the time they left for Ottawa.
I think we need to look no further than the front page of the Financial Times, which states it is Canada's newspaper for investment, to ascertain that they congratulate the government for having turned a deaf ear to deficiency payments. The article is headed "Deficiency Payment Denial Augurs Well". Then it goes on to say what they think about giving any subsidies to western grain producers. On the opposite page of the same newspaper there is an advertisement which probably gives you a better idea of what they suggest you should do, and that is buy British Columbia Electric bonds which carry an interest rate of 5.63 per cent. I think that this is their solution, and if it is then the government has given the answer that that is the best thing to do.
Let us look at what has been happening to agriculture in general. The dominion bureau of statistics figures on December 10, 1958 point out that the cost of living and production index for the western grain producers stands at 244.9, taking 1935-39 as equalling 100. In other words, it means that it costs the prairie farmer $2.44 for what one dollar would buy in 1935. This means that the $1.40 initial payment on wheat is worth only 57 cents in 1935-39 value of money, basis of No. 1 northern wheat, Fort William. This is equivalent to a price at a country elevator point of approximately 49.5 cents a bushel.
As has been pointed out, the western farmer is faced with a most serious position because in the period from 1945 to 1953 the cost of production had risen by 51 per cent. During the same period of time the price they got for their wheat went down by 21 per cent. This is an indication that something must be done for these people. I do not believe they came here asking for a handout. What they are asking is that some consideration be given to the fact that the Canadian government sells their wheat, and it takes some time

before they know exactly what they are going to get for that wheat. They now find that they are not going to get a price that is in keeping with their cost of production. They are asking the government, through a short range program, to pay deficiency payments for the last three years. I suggest that the remaining segments of the economy of Canada would look favourably on this type of payment. It could easily be pointed out that the farmers of western Canada are not going to be able to produce if they have not enough money to pay the expenses they incur in the production of that wheat.
We have assumed in Canada a responsibility for the marketing of their wheat. We have assumed, or we have neglected to assume, any responsibility for the matter of inflation which has meant that the money they have received has not been worth as much as it was previously. We have this responsibility, and I think we have a responsibility to the farmers of western Canada to see that they continue to exist in that area.
These farmers came to Ottawa and presented their case. I think they are going to do something else besides present this case. I am sure they are going back to their own areas and they are going to report upon the reception they received from the government as well as individual members of parliament. They have already one western member's report in this house that there was no need for this delegation to come to Ottawa because 47 Conservative members had been elected from the west to do the talking for these people. I feel these members are going to have to do more talking for the delegation because I think much more pressure is going to be put on them.
We have made inquiries about this dollar an acre payment versus deficiency payments. In no case did I meet a farmer who considered the dollar an acre payment to be a substitute for deficiency payments, and I did not meet any farmers who considered deficiency payments or acreage payments or both to be any substitute for a full parity price program. These farmers realize they can justify to the other segments of the Canadian economy their request for the cost of production plus a fair and reasonable wage. I do not think they are asking for anything unreasonable.

These are things that they will continue to do as long as they get a decent living. But when they are getting less than parity, they are going to produce surpluses because they are going to be obliged to produce twice as much.

On a number of occasions the minister has pointed out that the farm cash income is higher this year than it has been for a number of years. I think this statement is probably true. But I also think it is not correct to imply that the farmer has more money now than he had before. I think this situation results from the farmer having to overproduce, from his having to put in a couple of extra head of cattle in the barn and having to sell an extra couple of beef. I am sure if the farmers from western Canada were asked-and they should know about the matter-they would tell you that they have sold more beef this year than it has been their practice to do in the past because the price has been good and they needed the money, and this has raised the price.
I had some research done into the total price index numbers, taking into consideration the drop in the value of our dollar. Our deflated cash income from farm products, according to these figures has dropped 7.37 per cent. At the same time these figures also point out that comparing the average for 1946-1956 with that of 1957-1958, the farm cash income has risen by 10.26 per cent; the net farm income has dropped by 11.14 per cent; the deflated cash income from farm products is down 7.37 per cent; and the deflated total net income is down 34 per cent. Mr. Chairman, I think this is the reason why there has had to be an increase in production. This is the reason why there will be a surplus established with low prices and not with high prices.
Agriculture is faced with another problem that is almost insurmountable. We have it in eastern Canada. This may not apply to areas for deficiency payments. This situation may not apply to western Canada yet, although I suggest that they had better take a close look at it because it will affect western Canada shortly. I refer to the matter of vertical integration. A great deal has been said about vertical integration, some of it in a light vein and some of it in a heavy vein. I noticed in the Western Producer a short article on vertical integration. It reads as follows:
The most striking example of vertical integration is to be found in the northern Saskatchewan constituency of Athabasca,-

The quotation continues:
-says C.C.F. MLA John Harrop. One of his constituents raises chickens in an old mine shaft.
This is one aspect of vertical integration, I assume, because vertical integration means integration from the top of the bottom. If he has filled a mine shaft with chickens, I suppose that is vertical integration as far as the mine shaft is concerned. I might say that this is a new use for mine shafts.

Vertical integration in Ontario has become a major problem. I am told that the broiler industry is 98 per cent integrated at the present time. The pork industry is 30 per cent integrated and 10 per cent of beef production is involved in vertical integration or contract farming in one form or another. Vertical integration and contract farming are terms which are widely discussed and sometimes misunderstood even by the farmers themselves. I am told that vertical integration is the last stage of contract farming.
There are four major stages in contract farming. Many farmers have had to accept contracts because of their inability to get cash for such things as feed or the primary products and commodities which they need. The first stage of contract farming would be the feed companies supplying the money or the feed necessary to produce a particular crop. The producer is allowed to buy his own primary product and to sell it on the open market. Then he has to pay off his obligation under the contract. Interested in this type of contract farming are the feed companies, the packing companies, a number of industries and, also, a number of general stores.
The second stage of vertical integration arises where the feed is supplied under contract, and the primary product, too-the chick or the suckling pig, the small calf or whatever it may be that the farmer proposes to raise. The market is open and the farmer is allowed to pay off his contract with the money he receives from the sale of his product on the open market.
In both these stages marketing legislation would be of assistance and it is obviously to the farmers advantage to press the government for the type of legislation most suitable to his selling operations.
In the third stage of integration the contract will call for feed to be supplied and for the primary product to be supplied. In addition, there is an undertaking to supply the market as well. In this phase we find a number of the chain stores handling the finished product, and obviously in such a case as this it does not really matter whether there is marketing legislation or not, because it simply does not apply.
The fourth stage, which is total vertical integration arises where the feed, the primary product and the market are supplied and where, in addition, the buildings are owned by the company or interest managing the enterprise, and in which the farmer is only an employee or labourer engaged by the financing interest. I suggest that this last stage of contract farming or vertical integration will probably be the easiest to handle, because one of the enterprising labour unions will 66968-9-123i
Supply-Agriculture
organize these farmers and the farmers will finally end up with a decent wage and a decent standard of living. If this is the way the farmers want it, all they have to do is wait for a short time and this will happen in the province of Ontario.
Some time ago a young farmer from Almonte was in to see me and he told me that if the change to vertical integration continues in Ontario during the next ten years as it has done during the past three years there will be no more family farms as we know them today. I questioned two leading members of farm organizations about this-Mr. Hannam and Mr. Patterson-and neither of them would disagree with this statement, though they thought the process would take rather more than 10 years.
I think this is a very serious matter, and the minister should give earnest attention to it. If farmers are to be forced to sign contracts for feed, primary products and even markets, then I think it behoves the government to work out contracts which would be acceptable to the farmers concerned. In some cases where a farmer is in stage 2 of vertical integration, for example, the financial result may not turn out too badly, but in other cases the results can be disastrous. The same young farmer to whom I referred a moment ago told me of the experience of one of his neighbours who had entered a contract with regard to broilers. He had a thousand, and when things did not go too badly he was encouraged to go into the business deeper. He went into bankruptcy in two years in the sum of $57,000, and the reason was that when the broilers in his buildings were ready for market he was told: sorry, but the price has dropped, it is now 18 cents. Since this man's cost of production was something over 20 cents it was obvious that it was impossible for him to do other than sustain his serious loss.

speechtext:
I think I would be remiss if I did not speak on agriculture at this time because my constituency depends a great deal on the condition of agriculture. First of all, I should like to commend the delegation which has recently been in Ottawa on their able presentation of their brief and on their behaviour while they were here, and I hope that in my small way I can do something here, along with the other western members, to promote better conditions in the west both with regard to wheat and with regard to the general agricultural picture.
I do not wish to comment to any great extent on the remarks just made by the hon. member for Timiskaming. The hon. member talked about farming conditions, but I realized that he knew very little about farming conditions. He discussed contract farming and told us what a great threat it is to the farm industry as we know it today, and then he went on to cite a very good example of one of the dangers faced by farmers who enter this type of farming. It seemed to me that the example he gave pointed to the very opposite of what he had been saying up till then.
In western Canada we have two main sources of income-wheat and cattle. In my constituency we sell as much wheat as in any other constituency in Alberta, and probably there are as many cattle raised. On the average the farmers in my area had a fairly good year in 1958. However, they realized that this was due to the demand for cattle and to the relatively high prices paid for cattle on the United States market. They are greatly concerned lest this should bring a false sense of security to farmers in western Canada, because there is no assurance of a continued demand from the United States for Canadian cattle. It should be realized that apart from income derived from cattle revenue from all other sources is low.
During the past six or seven years there has been a great deal of diversification of crops in western Canada. The farmers went into the production of durum wheat at a time when the price of durum was slightly higher than that of hard spring wheat. Today the price of durum has fallen and we have a slight surplus of it. Quotas have been imposed on its sale. There is no longer any incentive for farmers to continue in the production of durum wheat to any large extent.
The same may be said of flax. Six or seven years ago there was a growing tendency to

go into the production of flax but today the price is down. Although we have disposed of some of the crop through the manufacture of linseed oil and exports the price has fallen very low. There is little advantage in going into the production of flax over the production of hard spring wheat.
The same remarks would be applicable to rapeseed which had a very encouraging price at one time. The price has declined to approximately half what it was and there now remains little encouragement to go into the production of rapeseed over hard spring wheat. I am pointing out these facts so hon. members of the committee will realize that with respect to field crops the situation in western Canada is somewhat serious. The prices that can be commanded for field crops are falling and the costs of production are rising.
On the one hand we have labour causing strikes and demanding higher wages. On the other hand we have management failing to take constructive action. The results of these failures fall back on the primary producer. He is the one who in the end has to pay for these failures. A good example of labour causing strikes and not caring one bit who suffers is the longshoremen's strike on the west coast last fall. It primarily affected the farmers of Alberta because to a large extent their early fall shipments of wheat go to the west coast. Some farmers in my constituency could not even deliver their initial quotas in the fall because the market was tied up on the west coast and the boats were not being loaded. Many farmers in my area were unable to deliver their initial quotas until January of this year. Incidents of this type have a severe effect on farm families.
I am a farmer and I feel qualified to speak about the position of farmers in western Canada. Farmers operate on borrowed money all summer. I would say this is true in the case of nine out of ten farmers. In the fall the farmers are in dire need of a little ready cash. When the initial quotas are not readily made available the farmers must obtain further credit and sometimes it is difficult to secure the "little more" that is required.
To illustrate how the primary producers are affected by labour I shall quote an article that appeared in The Rural Scene, volume 13, of June, 1958. This article considers the wheat pool figures in relation to the cost of a small combine. I emphasize that a very small combine is used in the illustration because most combines are much more expensive than the one referred to in this example. The article states:
In 1946 it took 1,845 bushels of wheat to buy a small combine; and today it would take 3,963 bushels.

And later:
II a combine cost 1,845 bushels of wheat in 1946 and the price of wheat has dropped 20.8 per cent since then, and if no other prices had changed, the present price of a combine would be 2,335 bushels of wheat, or 490 more than it cost in 1946.
That is due to the drop in wheat prices alone. I continue:
But the price of combines has changed, and now it is 3,963 bushels of wheat. This is 2,118 bushels more than it was in 1946. The drop in the price of wheat accounts for 490 bushels of this. The balance, 2,118 minus 490, or 1,628 bushels, is due to the rise in the price of the combine. This rise in the prices of the things he buys is what really hurts the farmer.
The article concludes:
The answer is plain to see. Labour costs have moved steadily upward ever since the war and they show every indication of continuing to rise in the future. Not only the direct factory labour but also the labour involved in producing the raw materials and transporting them. All labour costs have risen.
I cite this as an illustration, of another side of this picture. The farmers are concerned about continually increasing costs due to another part of our economy taking advantage of the primary producers. The farmers have to pay for this.
The cost of farm machinery in my area went up 6 per cent last fall and then along came the 17 per cent hike in freight rates. The price of tractors in my home town went up an additional $35 to $40 as a result of the increase in freight rates. While on the subject of freight rates may I say that I am glad to see on the order paper notice of the intention of the government to bring in a $20 million subsidy which will perhaps defray some of these increased costs.
During the last three or four years the price of tractors, cars, trucks and other large items that farmers must buy increased in my neighbourhood by between $600 and $1,000 and in the same interval, as I pointed out, the price commanded by field crops has fallen.
Labour is not solely to blame; management is at fault, too. Management has made no sincere effort to put out a machine and hold the cost of that machine. I do not know if hon. gentlemen are familiar with tractors but I will use them as an example. What have machine companies done in the past few years in terms of holding down the cost of the machines to a level that would bear some relationship to the price a farmer gets for his goods? They have continually changed models and designs. During the last four years they have continually switched from model to model and from design to design and now I notice that a tractor has been put on the market that has a two-tone paint job.
