This type of activity results in making it difficult for local agents to stock the many parts that are required for repairs to the machine.
During the forties tractors with rubber tires were put on the market. The fifties witnessed the addition of headlights on most tractors, individual wheel brakes and motors that would stand up fairly well to heavy use. There has been no drastic change in tractors in the past two decades. The price per horse power, however, has practically doubled. As. I said, the manufacturers are continually changing the external designs and we now have had the introduction of a tractor with a two-tone paint job that is perhaps no better than the tractors manufactured during the fifties although they have doubled in price since then.
I do not wish to dwell on this subject at too great length but I cannot resist mentioning that in my home town the farm equipment dealer four years ago sold more combines than any other dealer employed by that manufacturer in the province of Alberta. He was awarded a medal for doing so. Last fall this man had in stock two combines that were a carryover from the previous year and he could not dispose of them. I think he finally bought one himself at a loss just to move it. That is the type of problem confronting the dealers. Increased prices of equipment have meant that they are unable to sell the machines. A farmer certainly hesitates before paying $7,000 or $8,000 for a combine to take off his crop because although we have had fairly average yields in the last two years the prices commanded by field crops have been decreasing. This has to be considered also.
I have been told by one machine company that they have a price for machines which they charge in this country and another price which they charge in Europe, for instance. Those machines are made either in Canada or in the United States, taken across to Europe, and sold in that market at a much lower price than they are sold at in Canada. In other words, they have a two-price system for their machines, and this is very discouraging to the farmers of this country because they realize that the machine companies are charging just as much as the market will bear. Sooner or later the machine companies, for one reason or another, are going to price themselves right out of the market.
I think it was very evident from the delegation that was down here-I know the farmers from my constituency expressed it in various ways-that it is the cost-price squeeze that is the greatest problem so far as the agricultural picture is concerned. It is those irresponsible actions on the part of

Sup p ly-A gricu Iture
labour and management that have contributed to the continued high cost. Of course, the only way the farmer has to remain in business is to become more efficient. As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, some of them buy more land but that is not the only way in which the farmer can become more efficient. In many instances the farmer has ample land. He either steps up his production or the cuts down on his expenses. These are the only two ways that I know of by which you can come out with a higher net income. You either step up your production or you cut down on your expenses. Of course, if the farmers cut down their expenses very much the rest of Canada suffers to some extent through loss of labour used in producing machines or the loss of labour employed on the farms.
I should like to deal for a moment with the cattle outlook. Without a doubt the cattle picture in western Canada in 1958 was the brightest of any. The prospects for that crop were brighter than for any other crop the farmer had to market. Over the past year a great deal of concern has been expressed about the cattle market and about how long it will hold up. That thought was in the mind of every farmer who was down here with the delegation. They did not know. The cattle men are worried for fear the grain producers may go into the cattle business, produce cattle and thereby create a surplus. Of course, there is no way of telling whether they will go into that business or not. We have only to trust that in the future things will work out.
Let me go back to the fall of 1957. I think all of us from western Canada and eastern Canada will realize that in the early fall of 1957 we were faced with a depressed cattle market. Around October 1 the United States market opened up and things brightened up. Since then we have been in a relatively good position. It must be realized that in the last four months of the year we exported to the United States nearly 400,000 head of cattle. This was in the fall of 1957. In 1958 the number was around 700,000.
There is a great deal of concern in the minds of farmers as to whether there will be a surplus of cattle on the market in the future. The question is, how soon in the future, and what will be the effect on the price? According to the latest reports of the cattle population that I have seen the numbers of cattle are down below what they were in 1956. I think this is a good indication that perhaps a surplus of this product will be staved off for a while. The number of steers on the farm was down by 15 per cent. Calves were relatively the same as were beef cows also, although in some areas there
[Mr. Horner (Acadia) .1
is evidence that the farmers are reducing their basic herds. All this points to the fact that Canada, with a cow herd of about the same size as it was in 1957, can produce a great deal of beef if she is called upon to do so.
We must look at our population figures. We must also remember that from 1952 on, after the preceding fall in prices and the foot-and-mouth disease, we exported very little beef until 1957 when the vast demand occurred and we were in the very fortunate position where we could export beef to the United States. We should take a look at the Gordon report. This report states that by 1980 our population will be approximately 26 million. The report bases this estimate on the fact that our population will increase every year and that immigration will average around 75,000. Last year the number of immigrants was around 124,000, and most people considered it a low year. If one takes into consideration the increase in the birth rate and the fact that people are living longer now than they used to, I think it is safe to say that our population will increase about half a million each year and, of course, as our population increases so will the rate of increase. Therefore, I think it is safe to say that, judging by those figures, we shall very easily reach 26 million by 1980.
Of course, the Gordon report stated that by 1980 the numbers of our livestock would have to be doubled to feed our own population. If we keep these figures in mind, perhaps it would be safe to say that the cattle industry will perhaps hold up and that the next three years will be the crucial time. If we can hold on to the United States market for a certain small percentage of our production, then perhaps we shall be over the hump and be all right so far as cattle prices are concerned.
I should like to deal with hogs for a moment. We all know that as the price of meat goes down the rate of consumption per person goes up, and this has held true over the past years with hogs. Hog marketings have been very heavy, but we have surprised the experts. Through our own consumption we have got away with a great deal of this pork. Right now we have not much of a pork surplus. The price has been down to the floor. Anybody who has been watching the western markets particularly-I do not know what it has been like in the east-must have noticed that the price has been bouncing off the floor price at various times. I think in the future, perhaps by next fall, we shall see a trend upwards and away from the floor price of pork. Today, as I have mentioned, we have not got too great a pork surplus, probably one week's supply.

I think there is a great deal of concern among the people engaged in pork production, and rightly so, because with the floor price in effect there is the threat that contract farming will move into the industry. As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, they have already moved into the broiler industry and I am happy that we are not buying a lot of broilers. I think though that the government will have to bring in some sort of control. I do not know exactly how it may be done but the support will have to be reduced in the case of units that are large enough to be classed as contract farms. One way to do this would be by means of deficiency payments on hogs.
As hon. members know, the government is buying certain cuts of pork in order to keep up the price. In Alberta the price is $21.50 a hundred. If I were allowed to sell my hogs at 19 or 20 cents a pound, a deficiency payment to make up the balance would come to me. In that way I could sell 100 pigs and get a deficiency payment on those 100 pigs but I would not get a deficiency payment for anything over that number. I think this would have quite an effect on contract farming.
I do not want to speak too long but I think I should mention that I am certain the farmers will be pleased to receive the interim payment on wheat. Most of them should have received it by this time. I am certain that with the increase in the lakehead price of wheat of 5f cents the final payment will be as high as it was last year and perhaps a little higher on some of the lower grades. That is a very serious point. Last year the final payment on No. 4 wheat was just 2J cents a bushel and that had a severe effect on the over-all wheat price.
I am pleased to see that the port at Churchill has moved about 20 million bushels of wheat. Every bushel shipped through that port saved the western farmer about eleven cents. I would encourage the building of greater handling facilities at that port in order that the farmers can perhaps save a little more with respect to the cost of moving their wheat.
I think the government should be commended for the great effort made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in selling our wheat. It has played quite a large part in removing the surplus in western Canada. Right now the wheat board says that the grain bins will be nearly empty, and I think that is true. This has a two-fold effect. With the grain bins empty there will be no market for bootleg wheat and that will encourage those people who have gone into the contract feeding of livestock to get out of
Supply-Agriculture
that sort of business when they cannot purchase wheat at far below the cost of producing it.
I commend the government for the recent trade agreement with Russia and the export of wheat to Russia and Poland. I want to deal for a minute with tariffs. We heard a lot about tariffs from the farm delegation and it is true that the farmer pays the extra cost brought about by many tariffs. That being so, I think it is only right that the people of Canada should pay more for the wheat they consume in Canada. In other words, the farmer should have a little protection too.
A great deal has been said about what this would cost the consumer. I got figures from a well known baker. I am not going to go into the bakers' set-up at this time. This baker explained to me, by taking the number of bushels required to make a barrel of flour and the number of loaves in a barrel of flour, that the price of wheat could go up almost 60 cents before the price of a loaf of bread went up one cent. I think we should have $1 a bushel more for wheat consumed in Canada. This would raise the price of a loaf of bread by two cents. We must remember that the labourer today has never worked such a short period of time-

Mr. Chairman, the intervention in this debate by other non-farmers and nonexperts has encouraged me also to make a few observations about the agricultural industry. Personally I am not a farmer and there are only three or four small subsistence farmers in my riding and very few farmers in my province generally. The only personal connection I have ever had with farming was when I used to have to look for the cows and drive them home before going to school in the morning and then deliver the milk after school in the evening.
But there are several reasons why I should like to say a few words about this subject. In the first place I am deeply interested in the farmer as a human being and I also recognize the importance of the agricultural industry to our national economy. I am also deeply conscious of the deep similarity of the problems of the farmer and the problems of the fishermen who are my constituents. For example, both the farmers and the fishermen are primary producers. In both cases their production is affected by factors largely beyond their control. Both also are victims of the cost-price squeeze. Both are largely dependent on external markets and conditions.
In the case of the Newfoundland fishermen, practically all our fish is sold in foreign markets and in that respect we are even worse off than the farmers because our fish are sold to countries which have state purchasing agencies, which fact prevents the ordinary law of supply and demand becoming operative. Although we may have low production of fish in one year, the price does not go up because of the extra demand largely on account of the restrictions imposed by the state agencies which purchase fish in our foreign markets.
I think there is another similarity between fishermen and farmers and that is in their working conditions. Both farmers and fishermen work from dawn until dusk, but there is still a difference in favour of the farmer because in most cases the farmer can be home all the time with his family, whereas a fisherman has to stay out on the seas sometimes as long as two weeks.

speechtext: Order; I must mention to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that this is vote No. 1 on agriculture. I think I have been quite lenient in allowing the odd comparison between farmers and fishermen, but I must ask the hon. member to bring his remarks back to agriculture.

speechtext:
I was just pointing up the similarity of the problems faced by the farmer and those faced by the fisherman.

I am convinced that a solution of the agricultural problem is essential to the welfare of the economy as a whole. My final reason for entering this debate was that I thought members would be interested in knowing how farm problems appear to one who has no personal experience with them, and who has had to build up his picture from information received from various sources, including hon. members in this house. For 10 years now I have listened very patiently to hon. members tell this house about farm problems. I have read a great many of the briefs which have been presented to us by farm bodies. I have honestly tried to understand the problems and assess them in relation to the efforts that have been put forth toward a solution.
I should like to tell my farmer colleagues that this has not always been easy because the farm industry has been speaking, at least so it appeared to me, with two voices. I think there is a passage in the scripture which says that if the bugle makes an uncertain sound, who is going to get ready for battle? Well, there have been uncertain sounds from the agriculture industry. Farmers will tell us one story about blue ruin and the minister will get up and give us figures to indicate that things are a little better than they were last year. Certainly it is difficult not to be confused when you hear conflicting reports of that kind.
I think it should be pointed out that farm bodies who have presented briefs have painted their picture as representing the industry as a whole, and the minister too has spoken in terms of the industry as a whole without distinguishing between the component parts. We get two opposite and conflicting pictures and, therefore, we are reduced to the point of trying to put two and two together. Putting two and two together, it seems to me we must conclude that there is a group of farmers who are very poorly off; there is another group of farmers who are fairly well off; and in between the two there is another group who are perhaps just managing to keep their heads above water. What we do not know is the relative size or different categories of these groups. Neither do we know the relative causes for these different conditions. We do not know, for example, how many of the farmers who are in the poor group are there because of poor management or poor farm practices. We do not know how many are there because their farms are too small, and we do not know how many of them are trying to make a living from land which could be put to some better use.
I think this points out one of the weaknesses of the representations that have been made on behalf of farmers, and that is the absence of reliable statistics which break down the problem into its component parts. I am glad that

the farmers themselves have come to recognize this and have asked for research facilities. I would say the government should give them some help in acquiring these facilities. I think also the information should be gathered by the farmers themselves because they are in the best position to know exactly what information is required, and also in the best position to obtain it more quickly than could be done by a royal commission or some other agency set up for that purpose.
There seems to be no doubt that at the present time agriculture is undergoing a revolution, a revolution perhaps in many ways comparable to the industrial revolution that took place in Europe a century ago. While this revolution is going on the farmer is faced with three very serious problems, namely the cost-price squeeze; the problem of vertical integration, and the problem of surplus production. I think it is evident, too, that the measures which have been adopted in the past, as well as the measures which are in force now, have not been capable of solving these problems. I think it is safe to assume that in solving this problem, the measures we adopt will determine the future shape of the agricultural industry.
Since I am not an expert I am not qualified to make any recommendations of a technical nature, although I do not see why something could not be done toward remitting the sales tax on farm implements. It seems to me that the measures we have adopted so far have turned out to be merely stopgaps. What is required is a permanent solution. I believe that if a permanent solution is to be found, a whole new approach is required and a fresh start must be made. While I am not able to make technical suggestions, I should like to offer a few suggestions about the kind of approach I think is needed.
In the first place I think it must be a human approach. It is encouraging to find that the farmers themselves are coming around to that way of thinking. I was greatly encouraged by the brief which was submitted some time ago by the interprovincial farm union. That was the first time I have noticed an attempt to approach the farm problem in this way. The human approach requires a concept which takes into consideration the relationship of the farmer as a human being with other human beings and this approach requires the facing of certain facts.
The first of these facts is that price supports, deficiency payments and like measures have not proved to be a solution in the past and are not likely to be any more effective in the future and also that measures which are based on slogans such as parity,
Supply-A griculture
fair share of the national income and comparisons with tariff valuations, are in much the same category. All of these slogans mean different things to different people. Because of that fact they do not offer any basis for unity and unity is the first essential if we are to find the right solution.
The second fact that I think we must recognize is that whatever formulas are developed from the monetary standpoint they must of necessity be limited by what the national economy can support.
The next fact that farmers must face is that the government alone and the farmers alone cannot solve this problem. It is doubtful whether it can be solved by the farmers and the government working together. As I see it, the solution of this problem is going to require the co-operation not only of the government and the farmers but also of the consumers and, as the hon. member who preceded me in this debate pointed out, the co-operation of management and organized labour as well.
Another fact which I think farmers must consider, if they are going to get on the right track, is that there is no valid basis of comparison between the farming industry and the manufacturing industries in terms of monetary reward. There are basic conditions which must be taken into account. The farmer is obliged to work all hours from dawn to dusk while the factory worker works regular hours with a work week of 40-hours or whatever it may be. The factory worker is also more likely to receive higher pay for his services. It will not be possible to raise the farmer's income to a level that is comparable to the higher wage that is paid in industry. I think that fact must be accepted.
But the farmer has other compensations. He is engaged in a creative work, something which in itself must be extremely satisfying. It is a healthy work. He lives close to nature and close to his God. He enjoys a measure of independence which is not available in other forms of industry.
If the answer to this problem can be found only by the farmer, the government, management and labour all working together, then obviously this cannot be done without a basis of unity; and there must first of all be unity with regard to the goals and the objectives we want for the farming industry. This consideration raises the problem of vertical integration.
As I understand this problem, if vertical integration keeps on developing in the way it has started it will not be long before the only difference between our collectivized

Supp ly-A griculture
farms in Canada and those in Russia will be that collectivized farms in Russia will be run by the state and in Canada by big business. I think that is a serious trend. Even if it may produce some advantages in terms of higher production and lower cost, nevertheless we must consider whether or not that is too high a price to pay for that kind of end result.
Another essential in order to develop this unity is a recognition on the part of each party concerned that each has a responsibility to the other. Of course there must also be, in my opinion, a sense of mission. All industry has developed in response to human needs. The purpose of the farming industry is to feed hungry people. But if we are to develop the industry in the way in which its destiny requires, I think we must think of it not only in terms of a means of earning a livelihood but also in terms of something bigger, something which places the industry in proper relationship to other industries, and also in relationship to the world picture. What is needed then is a sense of purpose which will inspire in the farmer a sense of dedication which will largely tend to make up for any lack in monetary rewards. The working out of the solution between the parties concerned must take place around the conference table where each will be prepared to approach the problem honestly and fairly and in a spirit of what is best not only for the industry itself but for the country as a whole.
This will require some self examination on the part of the farmer himself. He will have to look back to see where he himself may have gone wrong in the past; whether he has exerted wrong pressures and whether he has been activated by wrong motives. In this way only can he discover to what extent he himself may be responsible for the condition of the industry today. This does not mean pointing the finger at one another, but it does mean an honest appraisal of the situation in order that we may not make the same mistakes as in the past. It is in this way that the farmer can make his best contribution toward a solution of the problems which face the industry and at the same time inspire the other parties upon whom he must depend to do the same.
There is one other point to which I should like to refer, and perhaps it affects government policy rather than the farmer himself. I refer to the need for a determination to use our agriculture industry strategically, as is done by the Soviet union. It seems to me that instead of giving cash handouts to the farm industry which may be paid for a limited period and then cut off, it would be much better if we could find some way of

expanding our markets. In Canada we have a very small domestic market of only 17 million people, but it should not be forgotten that Canada forms part of the commonwealth and that there are many countries in the world today which are potential markets for our wheat provided we go about the matter properly. In Africa, next year, Nigeria will become self-governing. Nigeria is a country with a population of 33 million, a very large potential market. Nigeria is one of the few countries in the world today which possess sound leadership and it is one of the countries which is going to determine whether the whole continent of Africa is to remain in the western camp or whether it will fall into the camp of Soviet Russia. We should seize every opportunity which presents itself to help Nigeria establish and strengthen her economy. I am told that in Nigeria a lot of the flour consumed is made from Canadian wheat milled in the United States. Why could we not establish Canadian mills in that country, either by private enterprise, or through the Colombo plan, and thus build up over the years an important market for our wheat? It is this type of assistance which will in the long run do more for the agriculture industry than any temporary expedients, however necessary these may be as short range measures.
In conclusion I should like to say a few words about the farm delegation which visited us a few days ago. This delegation focussed attention on the agricultural problem and deserves a great deal of commendation on the responsible manner in which its members presented their brief and also on the manner in which they conducted themselves throughout this visit. Not only did this delegation focus our attention on the farm problem but I think it served another and equally important purpose; it enabled us to meet a large number of farmers personally and thereby offered us the opportunity to know them as people and to appreciate their sterling qualities. The thought which has come to me since meeting some of these farmers-and I took the opportunity to meet as many of them as I could-was that the farmers may be the salvation of Canada, because it appears to me that they are the only group in Canada which has any vestige of a pioneering spirit. Some of us had feared that this spirit has deteriorated, but the personal contacts we had with these men showed, certainly in my case, that it is still alive. The farmers are one of the few remaining groups who are prepared to pioneer new territory and explore new trails even where it may have to be an act of faith. But the

farmers are tired of expedients. They want a permanent solution worked out around a conference table.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group of 73 over here do like the opportunity to get on our feet and say a few words occasionally. I sometimes wonder what we are here for. I have mentioned on a few other occasions what Prime Minister Macmillan said when he was here. It was something to this effect-I am not quoting his words-that if one were to believe what the press says or what the opposition says or what the government backbenchers say one would think that the whole country was going to the bad. And I am just wondering if anyone in this house thinks that this rump over here is a sort of opposition to the government. If we were, I think we could move a little way further down the house and get more accomplished with less talk than some of the hon. members to our right have been able to do.
There is one thing I should like to see, and that is this division line between the parties, this alleyway here, straightened out. There are four sections in here, and if they were shoved down a piece, and if the division line were put through there, there would not be so much difference. From time to time a member of the government stands up over there and says: "Hon. members of the opposition opposite", and sometimes he looks right at us when he is saying it and I know half a dozen of us maybe think we are Liberals, although of course we are not. However, I do not want to squeeze this side down too far, because that might shove my old friend from Kootenay West clear out of the door, and I certainly would not want to do that.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring a little more optimism into this chamber with respect to agriculture than I have been listening to on some occasions in the not too distant past. I wish first to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for the very fine summary of the work of his department he outlined as reported at page 254 of Hansard. The work to which I refer involved the expenditure of $186 million paid out by the Department of Agriculture as direct assistance to agriculture. This is no mean amount. This sum was expended in assisting in such projects as freight assistance on western grain, the payment of $1 per acre for agriculture which amounted to a total of $40 million-again no small amount-the payment of compensation for animal slaughter, the payment in the form of support prices on farm products, payments for grain
Supply-Agriculture
storage, P.F.R.A. payments, payments under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and other work.
I wish also to congratulate the deputy minister and the entire staff of the Department of Agriculture. I know something of the hours these men put in after work, particularly the employees of the experimental farm. It is my observation that they are a fine group of conscientious, hardworking men. I say this because I know something about the subject of agriculture. I was born on a farm in southwestern Manitoba and several years ago graduated from the University of Manitoba. Following this I worked at experimental farms at Lacombe and Brandon and after a very active life I retired for a few years. I then came to the House of Commons to rest and I find that just cannot be done.
There have been great strides made in agricultural research during all these years. It is a delight to me personally to know that the science services and the experimental farm services will be combined again in one complete unit. I feel that is a far more efficient way of operating these services. There was not very much duplication of effort under the previous setup but there certainly will be less now that their efforts will be united.
When I am on the subject of duplication of work may I say I think there is a little feeling among the people of Canada that there still is a duplication of effort as between the federal Department of Agriculture and the provincial departments of agriculture. I can assure hon. members this is not the case in British Columbia. There we have the university agricultural department, the provincial agricultural department and the federal agricultural department and far from there being a duplication of work there is a high degree of co-operation among these splendid groups of hard-working people. As I said before, I know whereof I speak.
No sooner is one problem solved in agriculture these days than a dozen new problems arise demanding solutions. Things are moving very quickly and so the world today is the product of what we believed yesterday just as tomorrow's world will be the product of what we believe right now. I feel that if we are to avoid the mistakes of the past, men of good will such as you and I, members of this parliament, regardless of which side of the house we are on, have a wonderful and challenging job to do. We must find the kind of leadership that will instil in the hearts and minds of Canadians the concept of true citizenship.

There is one other matter which I have contemplated mentioning but I do not know whether or not I should speak of it. I am going to mention it, Mr. Chairman, and leave it to you to decide whether or not I should have mentioned this point. It is evident that some hon. members in their speeches are talking to people at home having in mind the next election. I feel that by this time with the results of the last election well known we can surely forget considerations of this kind for a year or two and get down to the business we were sent here to conduct and stop talking about the past. After having said that and as I look around me I feel maybe I am talking to the people at home because there are not many hon. members present in the chamber to listen to me and I see many empty seats.

I think it is a waste of time to rehash political issues in this chamber when we know that the people of Canada would welcome the news of our putting our minds to the task of finding constructive solutions to their problems and getting on with the business at hand. I should like to quote from the Canada Year Book, 1957-58, page 119, with respect to agriculture in British Columbia:
The traditional movement of population on the North American continent from east to west has not been apparent in Canadian statistics in recent years. The most spectacular changes are shown in the prairie provinces and in British Columbia. While the three prairie provinces lost by migration about 250,000 persons between 1931 and 1941 and somewhat more from 1941 to 1951, they gained in the period 1951-56.
British Columbia gained at the rate of about 8,000 persons a year during the 1930's, about 23,000 a year during the 1940's and about 27,000 a year in the first half of the 1950's. On an absolute basis Ontario received more people than did British Columbia but, in relation to its larger population, this growth was only about one-third as important.
The importance of British Columbia's agriculture reveals some illuminating facts to which I should like to draw attention. Less than 2 per cent of the total area of the province of British Columbia is potential agricultural land and approximately only .5 per cent of this total area is now producing agriculturally. Less than one crop acre per person is produced in British Columbia. This is only about half enough which means that approximately half the food consumed in the province must be imported. Between 25 and 27 per cent of all agricultural land in the province must be irrigated. Agriculture in

the province is very diversified and any crops that will grow anywhere else in Canada will grow in British Columbia. In addition British Columbia can produce some crops that cannot be produced elsewhere in the nation.
The Fraser valley is one of the most important agricultural areas in the province. I do not refer specifically to my own constituency but to that area extending from Hope to the coast which is about 100 miles in distance. Thirty miles of this district in the upper end are not particularly agricultural but in the area that is approximately 15 miles wide and 75 miles long, 48 per cent of the agricultural wealth of the province is produced. Thirty-nine per cent of the farmers of the province dwell in this area and
38.5	per cent of all British Columbia farms are located there. The remaining 52 per cent of British Columbia's agricultural wealth is produced in nine other regions. The greatest of these is the Okanagan valley that produces about 18 per cent or a little less than one-third of the output of the Fraser valley. Next is Vancouver island with 10 per cent and the remaining seven regions with 25 per cent.
There is a substantial food processing industry in the Fraser valley. It is not generally known that in greater Vancouver food processing is second only to wood production in the number of employees it engages. The Fraser valley contributes substantially to this secondary industry. The Fraser valley produces 85 per cent of the total of the small fruits; 59 per cent of the provincial vegetables and potatoes, and so forth; 65 per cent of the special horticultural crops such as bulbs, flowers, holly, nuts, nursery stock, and so forth. So far as livestock are concerned, 66 per cent of the dairy production, 66 per cent of poultry and 61 per cent of turkeys are produced in the Fraser valley. According to the 1956 census, the value of the lower Fraser valley production amounted to $49,338,000. The amount for the other areas was $54,618,000, or a grand total of $103,956,000. These are 1956 census figures and are taken from the extension service bulletin published by the provincial department of agriculture.
I should like to say just a word about Chilliwack but I do not want to say anything against the rest of the towns and villages within my territory. Chilliwack, of course, is the centre of the area. There are 7,300 people in the city and there are 17,000 in the municipalities. Within a radius of nine miles of the centre of Chilliwack there are 25,000 people. In terms of retail trade, Chilliwack is British Columbia's fifth largest city. Three miles from the centre of the city is located one of the large Fraser valley milk producing

co-operative plants. The Fraser valley milk producers have 6,000 members. The plant nearest to Chilliwack is one of the largest on the North American continent. There they accept, in the rush season of the year, half a million pounds of milk per day.
I see my time is going very quickly and I know there are other members who wish to speak, but there are just a few things I would like to say at this time about British Columbia agriculture. I should like to take a few minutes to say something about some of the most serious problems in our area. Before I do that I wish to say that the dairy business in the Fraser valley of British Columbia is in a very satisfactory position at the present time. I should like to mention the raspberry growers. Those of you who heard me speak about raspberries a year ago will, I am sure, be glad to know that some of the growers out there are looking forward to a better year than they had last year. You will recall that last year berries were offered at six cents a pound. We had a nine cent floor put under them which saved the crop. I could quote some letters of appreciation for what the government did for the farmers. Strawberries are also a problem, not in their production but in getting a suitable price to the producer for his product. This should be in the neighbourhood of 17 cents a pound. Our poultrymen are also in a little trouble. Those of you who heard the minister speak some time ago heard him mention broilers. In 1953 I think some 30 million pounds were produced; in 1958, 180 millions pounds were produced, or six times as much. With such a large production the price is bound to go down. One of the things that is disturbing some of the growers in the Fraser valley at the present time is the frozen pea problem in relation to the entire crop.
I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying a word about the artificial insemination unit in the Fraser valley. By the way, this is just outside of my constituency but it is something that I helped to organize and I am very proud of the results. The first cow was inseminated on February 1, 1945. Two people were employed at that time; at the present time they have 27 employees and after 13 years there are 6,000 members within this association. In 1958, 31,803 cows were inseminated in the Fraser valley. In the Okanagan, 2,022 cows were inseminated; in other subunits in British Columbia, 4,619 cows were inseminated; and in the province of Alberta, if you please, 13,269 cows were inseminated from the unit in the Fraser valley. They have equipment and modern barns; they have a good office and they have good storage facilities there. Most important of all, they are using real top, high-class sires.
Supply-Agriculture
I should like to mention one other item before I close, Mr. Chairman, and that is the Canadian writers federation which met at the recent Royal Winter Fair. This is the occasion on which awards to press, radio and television are given. Three British Columbia writers won first prize in that competition. I take off my hat to and congratulate Mr. Armstrong, Mr. Leach and Mr. McPherson on the great work they did.
What about crop insurance? I know there is a difference of opinion about crop insurance. I think I know the minister's attitude and stand in connection with crop insurance. I have made a little study of this problem during the last couple of weeks and I have not changed my mind too much on the subject. Those of you who were in the chamber when the hon. member for York-Humber spoke about unemployment insurance will recall that she mentioned the fact that you did not insure your house against fire today and expect it to burn tomorrow; you did not insure your life today and expect to be killed tomorrow; you did not insure your car today and expect to dump it in the ditch tomorrow. You did insure your employment hoping, I presume, to be employed whenever you wanted to but, if not, you received unemployment insurance. Personally, I think unemployment insurance is overdone a little because I personally have offered unemployed men work and they would not take a job because they were getting unemployment insurance. I wonder whether the statement that Abraham Lincoln made at one time has any relationship to this? Abraham Lincoln said that you cannot help men permanently by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves.
I have another item on old age pensions which I would like to apply to old age farm people. I do not know whether I should take the time to do it but I should like to say that on our farms there are a great many elderly people, some of whom cannot work. I should like to see put into effect in this Canada of ours some scheme by which people living under certain conditions could apply personally to spend their security cheques outside of the country. This would be based upon financial reasons. They might want to go to live with a relative outside of the country. It might have something to do with domestic incompatibility; it might have something to do with health. I believe these people could be far healthier living in another country. I simply close by saying that I feel something should be done under certain conditions for our older people, if they make personal application to those in authority, to allow them to live in another country, spend

Supply-Agriculture
their money there and receive their cheques there because there are other people coming into this country who certainly do that and live here.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to what the member for Fraser Valley had to say, particularly in view of the contribution he has made to the development of agriculture in British Columbia as superintendent for many years of the Agassiz experimental station. On his retirement from that position his services to agriculture in British Columbia were acknowledged by farmers' organizations, by all sections of the communities with which he was associated and by farm and other newspapers of British Columbia. I am sure that the name of the member for Fraser Valley will be included in the roll of those who have accomplished much on behalf of the farmers of British Columbia, including such men as the late Professor Sadler of the University of British Columbia, the late Professor Boving, whom the hon. gentleman knew quite well, and Dean Clement.
Before proceeding with my few remarks I want to support the hon. member's representations on behalf of farmers in receipt of old age security payments that the government should give consideration to these people having the opportunity, along with others in receipt of similar payments, to spend their cheques in other countries. Very often when they reach the age of retirement it is necessary that they do so for health reasons and certainly for their greater enjoyment during the winter months in Canada. Having overheard the minister's loudly whispered remark, I wondered whether he was going to call me out of order for referring to old age security.
I rise to say a few words on these estimates as a socialist who realizes the need of long term economic and social planning with respect to agricultural policies in Canada. I am not one who underestimates the difficulties in connection with such an approach to agricultural problems or suggests that all our problems can be solved overnight. I am one who has a great interest in the maintenance of the economic family farm because I believe we should maintain the values that it has preserved in Canadian society and the diversification which is so necessary for the maintenance of a sound democracy.
I am going to illustrate my points from my experience at one time as a peasant farmer in the Kootenays and with long knowledge of the situation there. Agriculture in the Kootenay district commenced about 60 years ago. It was largely promoted by the needs and requirements of the small communities, mining camps, lumber camps and the stern

wheeler steamers that operated on the lakes. I knew most of the old timers who located on various relatively small patches of ground, cleared the forest and sold their supplies directly to the customers I have mentioned. I am one who remembers the clearing of almost the first acres of land for agricultural production, and it was no easy job. As a matter of fact, I represent a type of farmer who is more acquainted with the axe, the crosscut saw, now replaced to some extent by the power saw, and the walking plow than with large equipment although owing to the circumstances under which we live there is an increase in the degree of mechanization even on the smaller farms in my constituency.
If we provide the proper circumstances and the proper marketing facilities at a satisfactory price there is a great opportunity for agricultural development in the constituency I have the honour to represent. There is an opportunity for considerable extension of general farming and some stock farming. We talk about developing the north and the hinterland of Canada but we fail to realize what large areas of land we have in this country relatively close to transportation. I can take hon. members to one valley in my constituency where you can stand on a knoll and look at 10,000 acres of black, alluvial soil that only requires draining and transportation facilities. It is 25 miles from the nearest transportation.
There is opportunity for dairy farming to supply the growing cities and for extension of poultry farming and new efforts in fruit farming, having particular regard to the suitability of our district to the growing of a limited variety of apples, of cherries and pears particularly, and small fruit.
There is also opportunity for considerable extension of part-time farming allied to the forestry industry-I am very keen on that- and allied to the tourist industry. We have these opportunities in our district because we have the land, and provided we have correct land utilization these opportunities can be taken advantage of. In our opinion there is a necessity in Canada generally, not only in the constituency I have the honour to represent, for a land use survey conducted as a result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. As a result of such a survey there should be a planned and systematic movement of farmers from marginal land. There are persons in my constituency farming marginal land cleared years ago which should have been left in timber, and I am sure the same is true of other hon. members. There should be assistance toward the location of these farmers on suitable land which they can farm to their profit and

advantage. There should be a program of reforestation of submarginal lands. That would mean close co-operation between the federal and provincial governments.
To illustrate the opportunities at the present time, let me describe the Slocan valley. It is 30 miles long and contains thousands of acres of fertile bottom land. It has a paved highway throughout its whole length, power throughout its whole length and a river possibly an eighth of a mile wide in places flowing throughout the whole length. You have all the basic requirements of satisfactory agriculture. Yet this valley is largely undeveloped. It is inhabited at the present time by some of that well-known sect, the Sons of Freedom, and a few survivors of the pioneers who have stuck it out. I have written the minister about that problem, and something could be done about it if there was co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. A very large acreage could be brought into production quite close to the major cities in our community. I might say that at the present time we are only producing about 25 per cent of the farm production requirements of the people in our district.
Then there is the Lardeau valley with
16,000	acres of almost undeveloped land which only requires draining in some cases and clearing in others. We also have the Inonoak-lin valley, some 15 miles long. All that is lacking is transportation to markets and roads. It is simply a question of economic and social planning and co-operation between the federal and provincial governments to bring this land into satisfactory production, and it requires the co-operation of the local farmers' organizations, chambers of commerce and women's institutes.
So far as my constituency is concerned, all these organizations have full knowledge of what I am referring to today, are interested in the developments and are willing to cooperate with the federal and provincial governments to develop the areas I have mentioned. Now, in so far as land problems are concerned, we have still an abundance of land if we bring into production the areas now lying idle.
The next need is long term loans at low interest rates. Under present circumstances it is impossible for young people to go on the land, clear it and develop it or build the buildings without the capital. This capital can only be provided through long term loans at low interest rates through federal or provincial governments. In this connection, I should like to quote from the report of the royal commission on the tree fruit industry of British Columbia, written by Dean E. D. MacPhee, M.M., M.A., B.Ed., C.A., LL.D.
Supp ly-A griculture
Before doing so, I want to say that in my experience this report is the most able and comprehensive report made to date in the history of British Columbia with respect to all the circumstances surrounding the tree fruit industry. It costs $7, but it would be a good investment, particularly for any member from British Columbia, because it is historical, factual and the recommendations were made after a serious study of the whole question. In connection with what is required with respect to supplying capital, I want to quote from page 798 of the report. This is what the commissioner has to say:
Financial Assistance
In the light of these factors, what recommendations should be made?
1.	I believe that the fruit-growing industry should be maintained, and that the needed assistance requires action by both the provincial and federal governments if suitable conditions can be defined. From the standpoint of both governments, it provides the most profitable return available to the residents of these areas.
He is referring to the fruit-growing areas of the interior.
-Despite the fact that land values have risen in some areas to quite unreasonable levels, one cannot envisage any acceptable plan to make other use of much of this land at anything approximating these values-approximating the investments growers have made. Despite the long history of the withdrawal of farmers in other areas of British Columbia from fruit-growing, I am convinced that it is in the interests of the province and the dominion to keep this industry alive in at least parts of the Okanagan, the Similkameen, and in the Creston valleys.
2.	Federal program-Fruit-growing is an expensive business per acre in comparison with other forms of farming.
I have had some personal experience in that respect. We were a green English family when we planted the orchard, and my father ordered 25 varieties. Then, we had to regraft the whole lot.
The investment in land and real estate is unusually high, as is shown in table 9. The nature of the operation requires a high expenditure for labour; the amount of equipment required by even the most conservative managers is substantial; the period of waiting before a crop is obtained is unusually long, especially for the production of apples and pears; and the possibility of mixed agriculture is relatively remote. Assistance, to be of value, must therefore be long-term assistance, covering a period of at least 30 years, or the working lifetime of a grower. It must be at rates and under conditions which are better than those available through banks and mortgage companies.
Long-term loans by farm loan boards-Mortgage companies are not a major factor in providing long-term loans in the valleys, nor do I believe that it is to be expected that the chartered banks of Canada will relax their arrangements and terms sufficiently to provide the necessary capital for the rehabilitation of the farms. Short-term loans, whatever their value for growers of annual crops, are of little significance in an industry

Supp ly-A gricu Iture
where the product requires a decade to develop. If the growers who qualify on other scores are to be assisted, and I believe they should be, and must be, the funds that are needed are long-term loans.
I believe it is the responsibility of the federal government to reorganize the farm loan board and to redefine its policies in such a way that these growers are able to undertake the re-establishment of their orchards without placing them under the annual pressures that follow from shortterm loans.
The conditions under which, in my opinion, long-term loans should be given are:
This is the part in which I am particularly interested, and I support the commissioner's recommendations wholeheartedly, as a result of my own experience and knowledge of the circumstances.
(a)	The farm should not be less than 10 bearing acres, on soils and with climatic conditions that give a grower a reasonable chance of profitability. (In every area, however, there are planted acreages which never have, and never will, qualify under these terms.)
Those are the acreages that are planted on the marginal lands to which I referred.
(b)	Loans should be made only to those who have demonstrated managerial capacity better than the average of their district.
(c)	Loans should be made for specified purposes, each one of which can be identified and valued:
(i)	Replacement of dead and damaged trees.
(ii)	Top-working of trees to change a variety of low market value to more market-acceptable varieties.
(iii)	Replacement of obsolete varieties.
(iv)	Purchase of orchard land.
(v)	The purchase of special orchard equipment, including trucks (not automobiles).
(vi)	Land rehabilitation.
(d)	Supervision and guidance, such as has been provided by the Veterans' Land Act, should be made available, especially for young growers.
The commissioner makes that recommendation without doubt as a result of his inquiry and in ascertaining the numbers of people in the fruit-growing areas who have succeeded under the V.L.A. to a greater extent than they might have succeeded had no supervision been given under the V.L.A.
The provision of some supervision and guidance to young growers is important, and may be critical, and the combination of the V.L.A. service with that of the provincial horticulturists will solve some of the problems. The amount of equity presently required by the farm loan board before a loan will be advanced (35 per cent) is excessive. particularly in the Okanagan valley, where property values are high. If the proposals of the federation of agriculture were carried out and care taken in the selection of growers, I hope that the farm loan board would be prepared to increase the maximum percentage loan to 75 or 80 per cent.
I have examined the statement of policy on farm credit issued by the Canadian federation of agriculture, and believe that they have substantially indicated the changes required in the Farm Loan Board Act and its operations to make this useful to the fruit-growers of these valleys.

Mr. Chairman, the same applies to those who wish to engage in small general farming, livestock farming, small fruit growing and poultry farming in my district. I see that my time is going, so I shall hurry along.
After having provided the land and made capital available, in order to assure sufficient production, in addition to the type of supervision which is suggested by the commissioner, I suggest that very close co-operation is required between the federal and provincial departments of agriculture and the experimental farms. In British Columbia that cooperation has been quite good, as mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. However, in other circumstances, I understand there has been some overlapping. There is a necessity, in our district particularly, for a general soil analysis survey, owing to changing conditions of the soil. Even in the area in which I live you find climatic and soil conditions change in very short distances. There is not very much information with respect to some of the areas I am discussing now.
We could do with an illustration station. While the experimental station at Agassiz serves the Fraser valley and the experimental station at Summerland serves the Okanagan, our conditions in the Kootenays are very different. I am not suggesting the establishment of an experimental station, but I do suggest we should have an illustration station for the assistance of farmers. These stations would give some leadership and guidance with respect to breeds of cattle, with respect to varieties of fruit which would avoid wastage in unnecessary plantings and things of that sort, and with respect to plant diseases.
I want to have a word or two to say about marketing. I might say that the commissioner wholeheartedly endorses the marketing scheme of Tree Fruits Limited in British Columbia which comes under provincial legislation. After a most exhaustive inquiry and the hearing of witnesses in all parts of the interior of British Columbia where tree fruits are grown he supports the present plan for the marketing of fruit and makes some recommendations for improvement in its operation here and there. But I want to deal with one recommendation he makes with reference to marketing. As found at page 790 of this report he recommends as follows:
That the provincial government request an amendment by the governor in council to the federal order in council under the "Agricultural Products Marketing Act" of Canada to give the fruit board powers similar to those given it by the lieutenant governor in council in the province of British Columbia, and in addition the powers to pool and equalize returns on tree fruits sold in interprovincial and export trade. No change in

the federal act would be needed because it already authorizes the delegation of the widest powers to the fruit board.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that if we could get some planned over-all agricultural policy in Canada there is an opportunity in our district for the development of processing plants such as jam factories, canning plants and cold storage plants for the storage of livestock, dairy and poultry products. In British Columbia in my constituency we used to ship out some of the finest jam in Canada. There is a large market for jam in Canada. We have the soil; we have the young people and we have the ability but it is going to take some planning and some co-operation.
In conclusion, may I say this. I have hurried along in order to complete my remarks by five o'clock. I think it is necessary that some careful reseach be done in order to obtain accurate figures as to the costs of production of crops and livestock in various regions in Canada. We have the bureau of statistics figures. We had the figures given to us by the minister from his point of view. We have the figures provided by growers organizations or farmers organizations which on occasion make representations to the federal and provincial governments. I think it is necessary that we have some research done in this connection so that we may have figures which are acceptable to governments and to the agricultural producers as a sound basis for the operation of the farm prices stabilization act. In our opinion, Mr. Chairman, it is only by this form of economic and social planning in relation to agriculture that the future of the family farm can be assured.
I have hurried through my remarks, but I am firmly of the opinion that we are not going to solve this problem until it is approached from a completely non-partisan point of view. In my opinion, the objective is very much worth while. When one goes through the prairies and sees, shall I say, the ruin of the countryside by the development of these large industrial farms-the small rural communities being decimated, the country church and the country amenities being destroyed by this development-I think it is up to all of us, regardless of party, to use our influence in this parliament, in the legislatures of this country and in the various organizations to which we belong, working toward what I consider to be an extremely worth while objective, namely the maintenance and improvement of the economic family farm in Canada.

I realize I am a new member and perhaps not well versed in these matters. It has been the practice of this house to permit a member on his own to stand a bill or order for second reading without adhering to the rule and shifting the item to its proper place in accordance with the standing order. This is a privilege all hon. members have. I feel it would be very wrong to continue the procedure whereby an hon. member can remove the privilege of another hon. member. I realize I may be subject to being overruled by a member of the cabinet or by the house itself. If we allow a practice under which one hon. member may take away the right of another with respect to a bill which he feels is important and should move up in the order of business we will be adhering to a bad principle.

I believe the hon. member has a point. Our practice in this house as long as I have been here undoubtedly has been to allow an order to stand under this heading of public bills and orders if the hon. member in whose name it appears requests that it stand. It is true that the rule says that it may stand upon the request of the government. Rationalizing our practice with the rule as closely as we can I believe that we have assumed that if the government did not object to the hon. member's request to have his order stood and no objection was made it was assumed that the government had requested

it to stand and the item was allowed to stand, the order was retained and the order paper was printed in the same order as it had been printed before.
All of us in this house have been accustomed to seeing a great number of items under this heading allowed to stand one after another and appear again and perhaps allowed to stand a second day and again a third day and then come back and be dealt with in the same order in which they were originally placed.
If strictly applied the rule would require the leader of the house to say he had no objection to the item standing but I think we have fallen into the careless practice of assuming that he says that when he does not say anything. That is my interpretation of what has developed as our practice. Perhaps the more correct way would be for an hon. member who wishes his bill to stand to rise in his place and say, "With the leave of the government I wish this item to stand," and that would put the house leader under the necessity of saying "Yes" or "No" and the matter could be dealt with in that way.
As we have followed the practice to which I referred as careless, perhaps we should consider whether in the future we might be more careful of what the rule says. Because we have followed that practice I do not see how I can interfere with the order paper as it stands today. However, I will take the hon. member's point under advisement and proceed accordingly.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-17, to amend the Canada Elections Act (election expenses).
He said: The purpose of this bill is indicated in the explanatory notes and was also indicated during the last session. It is to have apply the same principle that applies to candidates and contributions to candidates to the contributions to political parties themselves and to require that political parties, like candidates in an election, file a statement respecting the contributions that have been made to them and the source and the amount of the expenditures.
During the last session the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) had a number of comments to make on this bill and on rereading his remarks of last year I was pleased to see that he indicated he
Canada Elections Act
would endorse it this session. He will now be able to deal with it.
We find that when it comes to election expenses the larger the country grows, the more wealth it has and the larger its population, the more money there is around and the more money is spent for election purposes by political parties. Some millions and millions of dollars have been spent in recent years. It is estimated that some $7 million to $8 million was spent by the Conservatives alone during the last election, and we are of the opinion that the general public is entitled to know what elements of society, if any, are attempting to subvert political parties.
A candidate must disclose the source of contributions made toward his election expenses. That being so, we feel that the same principle should extend to a political party itself. We all know the axiom that he who pays the piper calls the tune. I think the public is entitled to know who is paying the piper with respect to parties as well as with respect to candidates.
I do not intend to go into too much detail or make too extensive remarks on moving the second reading of this bill. The bill was dealt with to a degree during the last session and undoubtedly, as the hon. member for Edmonton West indicated at the last session, he will support it now in order to get it in the hands of the privileges and elections committee this year where we can go into it in great detail.
In years past there has been an unsavory history of contributions to political parties. We know that in some instances people who make contributions get the spoils, or get on the gravy train, if there are any spoils or any gravy trains involved. I would like to put it this way. I should like to point out what the application of the present act means and how it is complied with or not complied with, as the case may be. I should like to do that by making reference to the returns which were filed by some of the candidates in the province of British Columbia and then pose the question whether we should not have a little closer look at contributions which are made to political parties.
My good friend from British Columbia, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), filed a statement or his official agent did on his behalf. We find an item in the return having to do with contributions to the candidate's fund in that constituency, or toward the Conservative candidate who is the Minister of Public Works, by a Mr. Frederick Field. His address is listed as 675 West Hastings, Vancouver. He made a contribution of $5,000, which is a pretty substantial amount of money. We find that the same individual,

Canada Elections Act
Mr. Frederick Field, at the same address in Vancouver, made a contribution toward the expenses of the candidate who is now the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) in the amount of $7,675.88, which is a pretty hefty amount of money to put into a campaign. We find that this same individual, Mr. Frederick Field, paid to the tune of $5,000 toward the campaign expenses of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson). My good friend, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) also was earmarked for a contribution. He did not fare so well as the other three individuals; he got only $3,000 from Frederick Field. Here we find one individual in Vancouver who, from the returns that I have -they may not be all complete; he may have had made other contributions to other candidates-contributed over $20,000 toward the campaign funds or the campaign expenses of the four individuals I have mentioned who now sit in this house.
As one can appreciate, this is a pretty hefty amount of money. Where did it come from? We do not know whether he was handling it in transit from somebody else. Whether it came from other sources is far beyond my knowledge. Whether some consideration was given to Mr. Field himself at a later stage by this government remains to be appreciated by each individual in his own light, but we find surprisingly enough that Mr. Field who dished out these 20,000 bucks at least ended up on December 1, 1958, by being appointed as a director of the Bank of Canada and the industrial development bank on a temporary basis. He was appointed for a three-year term on the first day of March.
There are other items listed, large amounts of money, in the thousands of dollars, for other candidates. The attempt is made by candidates to list the total amount of their expense contributions as coming from one organization, from a constituency organization of a political party or from the provincial headquarters of a political party. The point is that the present provisions of the act requiring the candidate to file his expenses are not complied with. The intent of the provisions is not complied with. The individual candidate can list that he received $6,000, $7,000, $8,000 or $10,000 from a political organization and there is no indication as to the people who contributed toward that lump sum.
The intent of the act in the first instance was to require the candidate to file his election expenses and show who made contributions to his election fund. This has been overcome by candidates filing a report indicating that they got their money only from one source, that source being, as I said, the constituency association or the provincial

organization or the national organization of the particular party. The source might also be some other organization or individual whose sole duty was merely to handle campaign fund contributions from the central party and distribute them to the particular candidates.
The intent of the bill is to attempt to meet the requirement set out in the act at the present time that the public are entitled to know the source of campaign fund contributions. We will then not have in the future such cases as I have just mentioned where one individual can be listed by four separate candidates as having contributed $20,000 with the result that people wonder later, after that individual is appointed by the government as a director of a couple of organizations, whether or not there is some nefarious intent involved. I am not suggesting that there was but I am saying that people would probably ask themselves this question if they had known of the situation. It is something that we should attempt to overcome. We should attempt to maintain the greatest possible degree of morality with regard to political contributions.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Would he place in the same category the appointment by the Saskatchewan government of certain people, formerly colleagues of his in the house, to positions under the Saskatchewan government?

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING RETURNS SHOWING INCOMES OF POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the hon. member is not going to answer the question so I should like to proceed with the debate that has been initiated on this bill. The subject matter of course, is of very vital and deep interest to all hon. members because it involves a proposed amendment to the Canada Elections Act and each member of the house is very much interested in the contents of the Canada Elections Act as well as the operation of the statute because it is by means of that machinery that we have all found our way to this chamber as members thereof. The bill deals with one of the most vexing problems confronting any Canadian citizen who offers himself for office on the federal level, namely the processes whereby he obtains the funds necessary to run his political campaign. These funds are popularly known, of course, as the sinews of war.
As I listened to the hon. member explain the bill it seemed to me that he has a very dark and suspicious outlook with regard to the level of public morality in this country. No doubt he was speaking for himself and he is entitled to do so, but in participating in this debate I want to deal with my understanding of the bill before the house from my own experience as a candidate in several elections since 1951. Before the hon. member

spoke I had given him the benefit of the doubt and had suspected that he might be preoccupied with the problem confronting every member resulting from the rising cost of conducting election campaigns. I had thought that the amendment that he proposed to the act perhaps would make some small contribution toward reducing the ceiling on the costs of running an election campaign. However, in listening to his remarks I found that this idea did not enter into his interpretation of the amendment.
In a democratic society such funds must be raised from private sources. We have no access whatsoever to public funds in obtaining the necessary finances to carry on our election campaigns. All of these funds are provided through voluntary support. From my experience I have found that there are at least four major categories into which we can divide the sources of the funds obtained by the local committee, the provincial committee or the national campaign committee. First of all, some of these funds are obtained from large business corporations. Second, smaller business firms in the local communities make their contributions, usually on the level of the local campaign committees. Again, with the development of modern society and the emergence of other organized groups, labour unions have made substantial contributions to political campaigns. In Canada there is a tendency for this source of voluntary contributions to support one particular political group. However, from personal experience I find that the most important source of election campaign funds is contributions made by supporters of the party within the constituency, by donors who anonymously contribute to a particular individual's election campaign.
In addition, and I doubt whether this practice prevails in the larger urban areas, in rural western constituencies particularly it has become almost an accepted practice to help to defray election expenses by the old fashioned method of passing the hat or taking up a collection. By that means expenses arising from renting a hall are covered at the local community level. I know that in my constituency organization we try to make every poll in the district responsible for the expenses arising from the carrying on of the campaign in that particular section of the constituency. From my experience in several elections those are the main sources of campaign funds. As I examine the sources of the funds, I see no reason to be unduly suspicious that the contributions made are designed to subvert the true processes of our democratic society.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, I am speaking from my personal experience.
Canada Elections Act
However, if it is true that funds from these various sources are used as suggested by the sponsor of this bill for subversive purposes, it suggests an unfortunate level of political morality in this country, which I trust does not operate too generally or in too many constituencies. I have never observed that tendency myself, and therefore I have the feeling that the introduction, the interjection, the emphasis or the underscoring of this particular aspect of the problem of raising funds is a tendency toward projection on the part of the hon. member concerned.
I would have one very strong objection to supporting the amendment as it is outlined in the bill. The essence of our democratic system is the secret ballot. I think if there is any subversion involved at all in the situation, that subversion would occur as a result of the amendment. There would be a tendency to violate the principle of the secret ballot because there would be widespread knowledge as to the support of the private citizen, the business corporation or other groups I mentioned, given to particular political parties by the donors concerned.
