Although the hon. member did not mention this particular aspect of the problem, if the hon. member is concerned about the rising costs of conducting an election campaign I think there are other ways of dealing with the problem than the one outlined in the bill before the house. I am going to refer to the systems that are followed in the United States and the United Kingdom. A ceiling is placed on the moneys that can be expended by each of the major groups. Whether or not there is adherence to this ceiling, I do not know, but the ceiling is set at the sum of $3 million. In the United Kingdom, they have provided more direct control over expenditures. Expenditures are limited to so much per voter in each riding, plus a flat sum that is allowed for the national campaign.
These are attempts to cope with this problem by legislative means. In the United States, perhaps, the legislative approach has not been too successful. In the United Kingdom, I understand that the legislation is effective in imposing a ceiling. I would suggest

Canada Elections Act
that a much better, a much more democratic approach to this problem, is to operate a legitimate campaign. The old days of vote buying and other devices that used to be resorted to in the elementary stage of the development of our democratic processes, I feel sure are now past. We can further reduce the expenditure ceiling by encouraging voluntary workers, by resorting to old fashioned techniques of economy, by having the campaign conducted on a voluntary basis, party workers volunteering their services in all respects, the scrutineers manning the polls and so forth, which tends to be one of the major items of expenditure.
I think that rather than endeavouring to impose morality by legislative means upon the body politic, we would be making a much more substantial contribution to our electoral processes if we worked toward raising the level of political morality generally. It is well-known truism that stateways do not make folkways. You cannot impose morality upon the public by legislative means. If there is larceny in the soul, it will burst out regardless of how many legislative prohibitions are imposed. If my hon. friend is concerned about the tendency toward subversion of our democratic processes by means of the financial control exercised through voluntary contributions, I think he would be making a more positive contribution toward the solution of this problem if he campaigned on behalf of raising the level of public morality generally; that should be part of our election campaign in a democratic society. After all, those things that broaden the values, ideas and morals are not going to be controlled from without, but control must come from within.

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING RETURNS SHOWING INCOMES OF POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, time will not permit a very long debate tonight because we had such difficulty in deciding which public bill would be under debate. However, for the few moments at my disposal I should like to discuss generally what is intended by the bill introduced by the sponsor of Bill C-17. In the first place, I think I had better explain to the house that, generally, I am opposed to the legislation because, in my opinion, there have been too many attempts within the short time I have been here to make piecemeal amendments to the Canada Elections Act.
A brief review of the session just concluded will indicate to the house that last year there were five bills introduced, bills C-8, C-15, C-18, C-19 and C-23. The same bills have been re-introduced during this session. They are identical in form, and in fact they have the same sponsors as the bills that were unsuccessful in 1958. I am also of the firm
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
opinion that amendments to the Canada Elections Act are most important and should only be introduced after serious and careful study by the committee of the house which is responsible for that type of legislation, and after the advice of experts who are available to assist such a committee.
Another principle to which I am opposed, and which appears in this bill, is the infringement upon basic freedom. In the first place, the bill makes it mandatory that the return be filed within four months. If it must be filed, then it follows that it must be accurate. When filed it automatically becomes a public document. There are thousands of electors in Canada who make voluntary contributions of small amounts to political parties of their choice. I know that there are many thousands of supporters in the country who make personal contributions to the party which the mover represents. Equally, there are as many or more who make voluntary contributions to the party which I have the honour to represent. These people make these contributions on one understanding, namely that their names will remain secret.
As soon as a person runs for office he is marked and tabbed for life as a supporter of a certain political party. The same thing will apply if photostatic copies of the contribution list were made public in each and every individual riding. That is something that could well result if the central committee were obligated to make public its contribution list. In fact, in my opinion, this bill, if passed, might do more to take away our freedom than any bill introduced in recent years.
I know that the mover last year referred to the fact that similar legislation was in existence in the province of British Columbia. That may be so, Mr. Speaker. However, that does not mean that it would be good legislation for Canada as a whole. As the hon. member who preceded me said, the most important thing in a democracy is to make certain that the ballot remains secret as it is today. Otherwise we might end up with a one-party system in Canada as we see it, unfortunately, in too many communist countries.

If it were mandatory that the individual donor to a national political party have his name made public, he would automatically be marked, tabbed and accepted as a supporter of that party. There are today in Canada not only individuals but many companies, both large and small, which make voluntary contributions to election campaigns. Many of them, including individuals, make contributions to more than one party. In fact,

I think the major source of campaign funds is the money that is collected voluntarily on the local level. This bill does not try to find out the source of that contribution unless the contribution finds its way into central headquarters.

Central headquarters is the hub of any political party. Are we to be obligated by this bill to separate what national headquarters might spend during the time of an election. How do we designate what it spends for ordinary day to day expenses? I do not think any hon. member present will disagree with me when I make the statement that, in order for a party to remain national, it is necessary to maintain at all times active national headquarters. It is necessary to have a permanent staff. I believe that all parties represented here have such a staff. Staffs must be paid salaries. Headquarters must be provided for them. There is also the matter of the publication of literature. In my opinion it would be absolutely impossible for any national headquarters to separate what is actually spent on elections. In the party which I represent an election campaign goes on continuously.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that there are other hon. members who wish to take part in this debate. In conclusion I wish only to state that I am opposed to the legislation principally because of the fact, as I said originally, that I do not like to see such an important act being amended piecemeal from session to session without the research and study to which it is entitled. In the second place, I am opposed to the principle of making it necessary for a donor to have his name filed in a public document and advertised throughout the country.

It is hardly worth while, Mr. Speaker, in the short time that is available to me now, to make a start on the rather lengthy remarks I have to make in connection with this bill. However, there are two points which I perhaps might be able to make in the two minutes that are left to me. The first is with regard to the declaration of election expenses by a central committee. Apart from the fact
Business of the House
that it is rather difficult to define just what the bill means by a central committee-and I think this point was raised by the hon. member from Edmonton who spoke on the bill last year-whether it is the national central committee or the central committee of the province or of a local association, there is this difficulty and I fail to see how the bill gets around it.
I am not suggesting for a moment that what I am about to say will actually come about, but let us suppose that the Canadian Labour Congress determines, as a matter of policy, to support a particular political party. As I say, I am not suggesting that it is the case but am just assuming it for the purpose of making this point. Suppose this policy was written into their constitution. Suppose that policy and that constitution required the contribution by various labour unions across the country for the specific purpose of earmarking funds to support political campaigns of a particular political party, and I mention no party by a name. Then suppose it comes campaign time and the election is over and the requirement exists that the particular political party which I am assuming the C.L.C. is supporting must file a return under this amendment. All the particular political party would have to do, and still be fully within the terms of this particular amendment, would be to state that the source of their funds was the C.L.C. How does this amendment, in the light of the point I have just made, assist in designating individuals or concerns from whom these funds are made available to political parties?
